## 1. Chapter on Loving-kindness
## 1. Discourse on Loving-kindness
1. Thus have I heard: 
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks, "Monks!" "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
[A. Ni. 11.15] "Monks, when the liberation of mind by loving-kindness is practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, eight benefits are to be expected. What eight? One sleeps in comfort, wakes in comfort, and dreams no evil dreams. One is dear to human beings and dear to non-human beings. Deities protect one. Fire, poison, and weapons do not affect one. If one does not penetrate further (to the fruit of Arahantship), one goes to the Brahma world. Monks, when the liberation of mind by loving-kindness is practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, these eight benefits are to be expected."
Whoever, being mindful, develops boundless loving-kindness, for that person who sees the destruction of the bases of rebirth, the fetters become thin. If, with a mind free from ill-will, one develops loving-kindness even for a single being,
2:
one becomes endowed with wholesome states because of that. The noble one who has a mind of compassion for all beings performs abundant merit. Those kings who were like royal seers, after conquering the earth teeming with beings, traveled about performing sacrifices: the Sassameda (collecting a tenth of the crops as tax), the Purisamedha (providing salaries to employees), the Sammāpāsa (providing capital to the poor), and the Vājapeyya (speaking pleasant words), which allow the citizens to live with their doors unlocked. These (sacrifices and deeds of the kings) do not reach even a sixteenth part of a well-developed mind of loving-kindness, just as the radiance of all the stars does not reach a sixteenth part of the moon's radiance. One who does not kill nor cause others to kill, who does not conquer nor cause others to be conquered, who has loving-kindness for all beings—that person has no enmity with anyone.
The First Sutta.
## 2. Discourse on Wisdom
2. Monks, these eight causes and eight conditions lead to the obtaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life if it has not been obtained, and to its further increase, expansion, development, and complete fulfillment if it has been obtained. What eight? Here, monks, a monk lives in dependence on the Teacher or on a certain fellow practitioner in the position of a teacher, towards whom he has established an intense sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), affection, and respect. Monks, this is the first cause and first condition that leads to the obtaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life if it has not been obtained, and to its further increase, expansion, development, and complete fulfillment if it has been obtained.
While that monk lives in dependence on the Teacher or on a certain fellow practitioner in the position of a teacher, towards whom he has established an intense sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing,
3:
Love and respect are established [towards them]. From time to time, he approaches those teachers and fellow practitioners and asks: 'Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?' Those venerable ones reveal to him what was unrevealed, clarify what was not clear, and dispel his doubts about various doubtful points of the Dhamma. Monks, this is the second cause and second condition that leads to the attainment of wisdom not yet attained, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already attained in the beginning of the holy life.

Having heard that Dhamma, he achieves a twofold seclusion: bodily seclusion and mental seclusion. Monks, this is the third cause and third condition that leads to the attainment of wisdom not yet attained, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already attained in the beginning of the holy life.

He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and training himself by undertaking the training rules. Monks, this is the fourth cause and fourth condition that leads to the attainment of wisdom not yet attained, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already attained in the beginning of the holy life.

He is of great learning, a bearer of what he has heard, a storehouse of what he has heard. Those teachings which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings he has heard much of, retained, recited, mentally investigated, and fully understood with right view. Monks, this is the fifth cause and fifth condition that leads to the attainment of wisdom not yet attained, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already attained in the beginning of the holy life.

He dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is strong, firm in exertion, and does not neglect the duty of cultivating wholesome states. Monks, this is the sixth cause and sixth condition that leads to the attainment of wisdom not yet attained, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already attained in the beginning of the holy life.

When he has entered the Saṅgha, he does not engage in various kinds of talk or in talk that is contrary to the Path and Fruit. He either speaks on the Dhamma himself or invites another to speak, and he does not despise noble silence.
4:
Monks, this is the seventh cause and seventh condition that leads to the attainment of wisdom not yet attained, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already attained in the beginning of the holy life.

He dwells contemplating the rise and fall of the five aggregates of clinging: 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form. Such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling. Such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the passing away of perception. Such are mental formations, such is the origin of mental formations, such is the passing away of mental formations. Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.' Monks, this is the eighth cause and eighth condition that leads to the attainment of wisdom not yet attained, and to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already attained in the beginning of the holy life.

Fellow practitioners praise him thus: 'This venerable one dwells depending on the Teacher or on a certain fellow practitioner in the position of a teacher, towards whom he has established a strong sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, love, and respect. This quality of praise also leads to being loved, to being respected, to the development of the heart, to the attainment of the ascetic life, and to oneness. (1)

## 3. Paṭhama Appiya Sutta

3. Monks, possessed of eight qualities, a monk is unloved, disliked, unrespected, and unesteemed by his fellow practitioners. What eight? Here, monks, a monk praises those who are unloved and disparages those who are loved; he desires gain and honor; he is shameless and unafraid of wrongdoing; he has evil desires and wrong view. Monks, possessed of these eight qualities, a monk is unloved, disliked, unrespected, and unesteemed by his fellow practitioners.

Monks, possessed of eight qualities, a monk is loved, liked, respected, and esteemed by his fellow practitioners. What eight? Here, monks, a monk does not praise those who are unloved and does not disparage those who are loved; he does not desire gain or honor; he is shameful and afraid of wrongdoing; he has few desires and right view. Monks, possessed of these eight qualities, a monk is loved, liked, respected, and esteemed by his fellow practitioners.

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Dutiya Appiya Sutta

4. Monks, possessed of eight qualities, a monk is unloved, disliked, unrespected, and unesteemed by his fellow practitioners. What eight? Here, monks, a monk desires gain and honor; he desires not to be looked down upon; he does not know the right time; he does not know moderation; he is not pure; he is talkative; and he abuses and reviles his fellow practitioners. Monks, possessed of these eight qualities, a monk is unloved, disliked, unrespected, and unesteemed by his fellow practitioners.

Monks, possessed of eight qualities, a monk is loved, liked, respected, and esteemed by his fellow practitioners. What eight? Here, monks, a monk does not desire gain or honor; he does not desire not to be looked down upon; he knows the right time; he knows moderation; he is pure; he is not talkative; and he does not abuse or revile his fellow practitioners. Monks, possessed of these eight qualities, a monk is loved, liked, respected...
7:
He is also one who develops the heart. 

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Paṭhamalokadhamma Sutta

5. "Monks, these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions. Which eight? Gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. Monks, these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions."

"Gain and loss, fame and obscurity,
Blame and praise, pleasure and pain;
These conditions among humans are impermanent,
Not eternal, and subject to change.

Knowing these, the mindful and wise person
Observes the conditions subject to change.
Desirable conditions do not perturb his mind,
Nor is he repelled by undesirable ones.

His attraction and repulsion
Are dissipated and gone to an end, they exist no more.
Having known the stainless, sorrowless state,
He who has reached the far shore of existence understands rightly."

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Dutiyalokadhamma Sutta

6. "Monks, these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions. Which eight? Gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. Monks, these eight worldly conditions revolve around the world, and the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions.

Monks, for an uninstructed worldling, there arises gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. Monks, for an instructed noble disciple, there also arises gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. Therein, monks, what is the distinction, what is the difference, what is the divergence between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed worldling?"
8:
Pleasure and pain arise. Therein, monks, what is the distinction, what is the difference, what is the divergence between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed worldling?

"Venerable Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be well, Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will bear it in mind."

"Then listen, monks, and pay close attention; I will speak." "Yes, Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, for an uninstructed worldling, gain arises. He does not reflect: 'This gain has arisen for me; it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' He does not know it as it really is. Loss arises... [and so on]... Fame arises... Obscurity arises... Blame arises... Praise arises... Pleasure arises... Pain arises. He does not reflect: 'This pain has arisen for me; it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' He does not know it as it really is.

For that worldling, gain remains consuming the mind, loss remains consuming the mind, fame remains consuming the mind, obscurity remains consuming the mind, blame remains consuming the mind, praise remains consuming the mind, pleasure remains consuming the mind, and pain remains consuming the mind. He is delighted by the gain that has arisen and saddened by the loss. He is delighted by fame and saddened by obscurity. He is delighted by praise and saddened by blame. He is delighted by pleasure and saddened by pain. Being thus involved in attraction and repulsion, he is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say he is not freed from suffering.

But for an instructed noble disciple, monks, gain arises. He reflects: 'This gain has arisen for me; it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' He knows it as it really is. Loss arises... [and so on]... Fame arises... Obscurity arises... Blame arises... Praise arises... Pleasure arises... Pain arises. He reflects: 'This pain has arisen for me; it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' He knows it as it really is. For that instructed noble disciple, gain does not remain consuming the mind, loss does not remain consuming the mind, fame does not remain consuming the mind, obscurity does not remain consuming the mind,
9:
Blame does not remain taking possession of the mind; praise does not remain taking possession of the mind; pleasure does not remain taking possession of the mind; pain does not remain taking possession of the mind. That noble disciple does not rejoice when gain arises, nor is he dejected when there is loss. He does not rejoice when fame arises, nor is he dejected when there is obscurity. He does not rejoice when praise arises, nor is he dejected when there is blame. He does not rejoice when pleasure arises, nor is he dejected when there is pain. Having thus abandoned both approval and aversion, that noble disciple is freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair. I say he is freed from the mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the distinction, this is the excellence, this is the difference between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed worldling.

Gain and loss, fame and obscurity,
Blame and praise, pleasure and pain;
These conditions among humans are impermanent,
Transient, and subject to change.

Knowing these, the mindful wise person
Contemplates their changing nature.
Desirable conditions do not disturb his mind,
Nor is he repelled by undesirable ones.

His approval and aversion
Are dispersed and come to an end; they exist no more.
Having known the state that is stainless and sorrowless,
He who has gone to the further shore of existence understands it well.

The Sixth Sutta.

## 7. Devadatta-vipatti Sutta

7. On one occasion, the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha on the Gijjhakūṭa hill, not long after Devadatta had left. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning Devadatta: "It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect on his own failure. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect on another's failure. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect on his own success. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect on another's success."
10:
"It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to reflect on another's success. Overcome by eight unwholesome things, his mind taking possession of them, Devadatta is destined for the state of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an aeon, incurable.

What are the eight? Overcome by gain, bhikkhus, his mind taking possession of it, Devadatta is destined for the state of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an aeon, incurable. Overcome by loss, bhikkhus... fame, bhikkhus... obscurity, bhikkhus... honor, bhikkhus... lack of honor, bhikkhus... evil desire, bhikkhus... overcome by evil friendship, bhikkhus, his mind taking possession of it, Devadatta is destined for the state of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an aeon, incurable. Overcome by these eight unwholesome things, his mind taking possession of them, Devadatta is destined for the state of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an aeon, incurable.

It is good, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu should dwell having overcome and overcome arisen gain. He should dwell having overcome and overcome arisen loss... fame... obscurity... honor... lack of honor... evil desire... he should dwell having overcome and overcome arisen evil friendship.

For what reason, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu dwell having overcome and overcome arisen gain... loss... fame... obscurity... honor... lack of honor... evil desire... arisen evil friendship?

Bhikkhus, for one who dwells without overcoming arisen gain, taints and the fevers of distress might arise. For one who dwells having overcome arisen gain, those taints and fevers of distress do not arise. Bhikkhus, for one who dwells without overcoming arisen loss... fame... obscurity... honor... lack of honor... evil desire... for one who dwells without overcoming arisen evil friendship, taints and the fevers of distress might arise. For one who dwells having overcome arisen evil friendship, those taints and fevers of distress do not arise. It is for this reason, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu should dwell having overcome and overcome arisen gain... loss... fame... obscurity... honor... lack of honor... evil desire... he should dwell having overcome and overcome arisen evil friendship."
11:
Monks, therefore, in this teaching, you should train yourselves thus: 'We will live repeatedly overcoming arisen gain; repeatedly overcoming arisen loss... [...] ...repeatedly overcoming arisen fame; repeatedly overcoming arisen obscurity; repeatedly overcoming arisen honor; repeatedly overcoming arisen dishonor; repeatedly overcoming arisen evil desire; repeatedly overcoming arisen evil friendship.' Monks, thus should you train yourselves," (the Buddha said).

The Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Uttara Vipatti Sutta

8. At one time, the Venerable Uttara was staying at the Vaᙩajālikā Monastery on Saṅkheyyaka Mountain in the Mahisavatthu region. There, the Venerable Uttara addressed the monks: "Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on his own failure. Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on others' failure. Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on his own success. Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on others' success."

At that time, Vessavaṇa, the Great King, was traveling from the north to the south on some business. Vessavaṇa, the Great King, heard the sound of the Dhamma as the Venerable Uttara was teaching the monks at the Vaᙩajālikā Monastery on Saṅkheyyaka Mountain in the Mahisavatthu region: "Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on his own failure. Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on others' failure. Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on his own success. Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on others' success."

Then Vessavaṇa, the Great King—just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm—disappeared from the Vaᙩajālikā Monastery on Saṅkheyyaka Mountain in the Mahisavatthu region and appeared among the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Then Vessavaṇa, the Great King, approached Sakka, the Lord of Devas, and said to him: "Please know, Lord Sakka! That Venerable Uttara is teaching the monks at the Vaᙩajālikā Monastery on Saṅkheyyaka Mountain in the Mahisavatthu region thus: 'Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on his own failure. Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on others' failure. Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on his own success. Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on others' success.'"

Then Sakka, the Lord of Devas—just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm—disappeared from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and appeared before the Venerable Uttara at the Vaᙩajālikā Monastery on Saṅkheyyaka Mountain in the Mahisavatthu region.
12:
Then Sakka, the Lord of Devas, approached the Venerable Uttara, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing there, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, said to the Venerable Uttara: "Is it true, Bhante, that the Venerable Uttara teaches the monks thus: 'Friends, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on his own failure; from time to time on others' failure... [...] ...on his own success... [...] ...on others' success'?" "It is so, Lord of Devas." "But Bhante, is this teaching the Venerable Uttara's own inspiration, or is it the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?"

"In that case, Lord of Devas, I will give you a simile. For in this world, some wise men understand the meaning of what is said by means of a simile. Suppose, Lord of Devas, there was a great heap of grain not far from a village or a town. A large crowd of people would carry away grain from it—with poles, baskets, in their laps, or in their cupped hands. Lord of Devas, if someone were to approach that crowd and ask, 'From where do you bring this grain?', how would that crowd answer so as to be answering correctly?"

"Bhante, if that crowd were to answer, 'We bring it from that great heap of grain,' they would be answering correctly."

"Even so, Lord of Devas, whatever is well-spoken is all the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Drawing from that word of the Blessed One, we and others speak."

"It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante! How well this was said by the Venerable Uttara: 'Whatever is well-spoken is all the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Drawing from that word of the Blessed One, we and others speak.' Venerable Uttara, at one time, the Blessed One was staying at Gijjhakūᙩa Mountain in Rājagaha, not long after Devadatta had left. On that occasion, the Blessed One addressed the monks concerning Devadatta: 'Monks, it is good for a monk to reflect from time to time on his own failure,'"
13: Monks, it is good for a bhikkhu to reflect from time to time on the failure of others... on his own success... on the success of others. Monks, Devadatta, being overcome and his mind completely possessed by eight unwholesome things, is destined for the state of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an aeon, and is incurable. What are the eight? Monks, Devadatta, being overcome and his mind completely possessed by gain, is destined for the state of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an aeon, and is incurable. Monks, [being overcome by] loss... fame... obscurity... honor... lack of honor... evil desires... evil friendship, Devadatta, being overcome and his mind completely possessed, is destined for the state of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an aeon, and is incurable. Monks, being overcome and his mind completely possessed by these eight unwholesome things, Devadatta is destined for the state of deprivation, destined for hell, remaining there for an aeon, and is incurable. Monks, it is good for a bhikkhu to dwell having overcome and overcome arisen gain; to dwell having overcome and overcome arisen loss... arisen fame... arisen obscurity... arisen honor... arisen lack of honor... arisen evil desires... arisen evil friendship. Monks, for what special benefit should a bhikkhu dwell having overcome and overcome arisen gain? [For what benefit should he dwell] having overcome and overcome arisen loss... arisen fame... arisen obscurity... arisen honor... arisen lack of honor... arisen evil desires... arisen evil friendship? Monks, for one who dwells without overcoming arisen gain, taints and the fever of distress might arise; but for one who dwells having overcome arisen gain, those taints and the fever of distress do not arise. Monks, for one who dwells without overcoming arisen loss... fame... obscurity... honor... lack of honor... evil desires... arisen evil friendship, taints and the fever of distress might arise;
14:
For that monk who lives repeatedly overcoming the arisen evil friendship, the taints (āsavas) and the distress of defilements do not arise through this cause. Monks, depending on this special benefit, a monk should live repeatedly overcoming arisen gain, arisen loss... arisen fame, arisen obscurity... arisen honor, arisen lack of honor... arisen evil desire, and arisen evil friendship. 

"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We will live repeatedly overcoming arisen gain, arisen loss... arisen fame, arisen obscurity... arisen honor, arisen lack of honor... arisen evil desire, and arisen evil friendship.' Thus, monks, should you train," the Buddha said.

"Venerable Uttara, among humans there are these four assemblies: monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. This Dhamma teaching has not been established in any other assembly. Venerable, may the venerable Uttara learn this Dhamma teaching. Venerable, may the venerable Uttara master this Dhamma teaching. Venerable, may the venerable Uttara bear in mind this Dhamma teaching. Venerable, this Dhamma teaching is beneficial and is fundamental to the holy life."

The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Nanda Sutta

9. "Monks, if one were to say of Nanda, 'He is a man of noble birth,' one would be speaking rightly. Monks, if one were to say of Nanda, 'He is strong,' one would be speaking rightly. Monks, if one were to say of Nanda, 'He is handsome,' one would be speaking rightly. Monks, if one were to say of Nanda, 'He is full of passion,' one would be speaking rightly. Monks, Nanda guards the doors of his sense faculties, knows moderation in eating, is devoted to wakefulness, and is possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension. What other reason is there than these—guarding the sense doors and so forth—by which Nanda is able to lead the holy life perfectly and purely?

Monks, among those four, this is Nanda's guarding of the doors of the sense faculties: Monks, if Nanda intends to look directly towards the eastern direction, he looks towards the eastern direction having focused his whole mind, thinking: 'While I am looking directly towards the eastern direction, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection will not flow in upon me.' Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard."
15:
Monks, if Nanda should look directly to the west... [etc.] ...to the north... to the south... look up... look down... look obliquely; Nanda looks obliquely after having attended to everything with his mind, thinking: 'While I am looking obliquely in this way, evil unwholesome states of covetousness (abhijjhā) and displeasure (domanassa) will not follow me.' Thus, he is clearly comprehending (sampajāna) in that regard. Monks, this is Nanda's guarding of the doors of the sense faculties.

Monks, among those four, this is Nanda's moderation in eating. Here, monks, Nanda partakes of food reflecting wisely: 'Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for ornament, not for beautification, but only for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, thinking: "Thus I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings; and I shall have sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable abiding."' Monks, this is Nanda's moderation in eating.

Monks, among those four, this is Nanda's devotion to wakefulness. Here, monks, during the day, Nanda purifies his mind from obstructive hindrances (nīvaraṇa) while walking back and forth and sitting. During the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind from obstructive hindrances while walking back and forth and sitting. During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion's posture, placing one foot on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having the thought of rising in mind. During the last watch of the night, having risen early, he purifies his mind from obstructive hindrances while walking back and forth and sitting. Monks, this is Nanda's devotion to wakefulness.

Monks, among those four, this is Nanda's possession of mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña). Here, monks, for Nanda, feelings (vedanā) arise known, persist known, and reach their end known. Perceptions (saññā)... [etc.] ...Thoughts (vitakka)... [etc.] ...reach their end known. Monks, this is Nanda's possession of mindfulness and clear comprehension.

Monks, Nanda guards the doors of the sense faculties, is moderate in eating, is devoted to wakefulness, and is possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension. Since Nanda is able to lead the holy life perfectly and purely because of these factors such as guarding the sense faculties, what use is there in mentioning any other reason? (Thus he said.) The Ninth.
16:
The Ninth Sutta.
## 10. Kāraṇḍava Sutta
10. On one occasion, the Blessed One was dwelling on the bank of the Gaggarā Lake in Campā. At that time, the monks accused a monk of an offense (āpatti). When that monk was accused of an offense by the monks, he prevaricated, led the talk aside, and manifested anger, hatred, and resentment. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, expel this person from the Dispensation. Monks, expel this person from the Dispensation. Monks, such a person should be removed. What use do you have for this person, the disciple of another, who has been cleared out?

Monks, in this Dispensation, the going forward, returning, looking ahead, looking aside, bending, stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes of some person are just like those of other good monks, as long as the monks do not see his offense. But when the monks see his offense, they know him thus: 'This one is a corrupter of recluses, the chaff of a recluse, the rubbish of a recluse.' Knowing him thus, they expel and destroy him from the outside. For what reason? Thinking: 'May he not corrupt other good monks.'

Monks, for example, in a fertile barley field, a plant might grow that is a destroyer of barley, the chaff of barley, the rubbish of barley. As long as its head has not emerged, its root is just like that of other good barley; its stalk is just like that of other good barley; its leaf is just like that of other good barley. But when the head emerges, they know it thus: 'This plant is a destroyer of barley, the chaff of barley, the rubbish of barley.' Knowing it thus, they uproot it along with its roots and throw it outside the barley field. For what reason? Thinking: 'May it not corrupt other good barley.' In the same way, monks, in this Dispensation, the going forward, returning, looking ahead, looking aside, bending, stretching, and wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes of some person are just like those of other good monks, as long as the monks do not see his offense. But when the monks see his offense, they know him thus: 'This one is a corrupter of recluses, the chaff of a recluse, the rubbish of a recluse.'
17:
Having known him thus, they expel him from the community. For what reason? With the thought, 'Let him not corrupt other good monks.'

Monks, it is like this: when a large heap of grain is being winnowed, those grains that are firm and possess substance form a pile in one place. But those grains that are weak and mere chaff, the wind blows them away to one side. The owners of the grain, taking a broom, sweep them away even further. For what reason? With the thought, 'Let them not spoil the other good grain.'

In the same way, monks, in this teaching, the coming and going, looking ahead and looking aside, bending and stretching, and the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes of a certain person appear just like those of other good monks, as long as the monks do not see his offense. But when the monks see his offense, they know him thus: 'This person is a corrupter of monks, a piece of chaff among monks, rubbish among monks.' Having known him thus, they expel him from the community. For what reason? With the thought, 'Let him not corrupt other good monks.'

Monks, it is like this: a man in need of a water-conduit for a well might enter a forest taking a sharp axe. He would strike tree after tree with the back of the axe. When those trees that are firm and possess substance are struck with the back of the axe, they give a hard, resonant sound. But those trees that are rotten within, moldy, and full of refuse, when struck with the back of the axe, give a dull thud. He cuts such a tree at the root; having cut it at the root, he cuts it at the top; having cut it at the top, he thoroughly cleans the inside; having thoroughly cleaned the inside, he fits it as a water-conduit for the well.

In the same way, monks, in this teaching, the coming and going, looking ahead and looking aside, bending and stretching, and the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes of a certain person appear just like those of other good monks, as long as the monks do not see his offense. But when the monks see his offense, they know him thus—
18:
—they know him thus: 'This person is a corrupter of monks, a piece of chaff among monks, rubbish among monks.' Having known him thus, they expel him from the community. For what reason? With the thought, 'Let him not corrupt other good monks.'

'Through living together, one may know: this one has evil desires, is prone to anger, is a denigrator, is stubborn, and is envious; he is jealous, stingy, and crafty.

He is soft-spoken in the midst of the crowd, speaking like a good monk; but in secret, he performs [evil] deeds, having evil views and no respect.

He is wavering and a liar. Having known him as he truly is, all being in harmony, you should expel him.

Expel the rubbish; remove the refuse. Then drive away the chaff—those who are not monks but imagine themselves to be monks.

Having expelled those of evil desires and evil conduct, you who are pure, dwell together with the pure, being mindful.

Then, being in harmony and prudent, you will make an end of suffering.'

The tenth sutta.
The first chapter, the Metta Vagga, is finished.

The summary of it:
Metta, Paññā, two on Piya, two on Loka, two on Vipatti, Devadatta, Uttara, Nanda, and the one on Karandava.

## 2. Maha Vagga
## 1. Veranja Sutta

11. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Veranjā, near the Naleru Neem tree. Then the brahmin Veranja approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. Having concluded the greetings and cordial talk, the brahmin Veranja sat to one side and said to the Blessed One: 'Master Gotama, I have heard this...'
19:
"I have heard this, Master Gotama: 'The ascetic Gotama does not bow to, rise for, or invite with a seat those brahmins who are old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, and reached the final stage of life.' Master Gotama, that which I have heard is indeed true. Master Gotama, you do not bow to, rise for, or invite with a seat those brahmins who are old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, and reached the final stage of life. Master Gotama, this is certainly not proper," he said.

Brahmin, I do not see anyone in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, whom I should bow to, rise for, or invite with a seat. Brahmin, if the Tathāgata were to bow to, rise for, or invite with a seat anyone, that person's head would fall off.

"Master Gotama is tasteless (arasarūpa)," said the brahmin.

Brahmin, there is indeed a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is tasteless.' Brahmin, those tastes for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and are not subject to future arising. Brahmin, in this way one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is tasteless,' but not in the sense that you mean. (1)

"Master Gotama is without enjoyment (nibbhoga)," said the brahmin.

Brahmin, there is indeed a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is without enjoyment.' Brahmin, those enjoyments of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and are not subject to future arising. Brahmin, in this way one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is without enjoyment,' but not in the sense that you mean. (2)

"Master Gotama is a teacher of non-action (akiriyavāda)," said the brahmin.

Brahmin, there is indeed a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of non-action.' Brahmin, I teach non-action regarding bodily misconduct,
20:
verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; I teach non-action regarding many kinds of evil, unwholesome states. Brahmin, in this way one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of non-action,' but not in the sense that you mean. (3)

"Master Gotama is a teacher of annihilation (ucchedavāda)," said the brahmin.

Brahmin, there is indeed a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of annihilation.' Brahmin, I teach the annihilation of greed, hatred, and delusion; I teach the annihilation of many kinds of evil, unwholesome states. Brahmin, in this way one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of annihilation,' but not in the sense that you mean. (4)

"Master Gotama is one who is disgusted (jegucchī)," said the brahmin.

Brahmin, there is indeed a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is one who is disgusted.' Brahmin, I am disgusted by bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; I am disgusted by the attainment of many kinds of evil, unwholesome states. Brahmin, in this way one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is one who is disgusted,' but not in the sense that you mean. (5)

"Master Gotama is a destroyer (venayika)," said the brahmin.

Brahmin, there is indeed a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer.' Brahmin, I teach the Dhamma for the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion; I teach the Dhamma for the destruction of many kinds of evil, unwholesome states. Brahmin, in this way one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer,' but not in the sense that you mean. (6)

"Master Gotama is an ascetic (tapassī)," said the brahmin.

Brahmin, there is indeed a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic.' Brahmin, I teach that bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, and many kinds of evil, unwholesome states are states that burn (tapaniya). Brahmin, for one who has abandoned the evil, unwholesome states that burn, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, done away with them, and made them not subject to future arising,
21:
I call one who has the nature of burning away [unwholesome states] a 'tapassī' (ardent one). Brahmin, the Tathāgata has abandoned evil unwholesome states—bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, rendered them non-existent, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. In this sense, Brahmin, one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a tapassī,' but not in the sense that you mean. (7)

'The venerable Gotama is apagabbha (not fit to reach heaven),' [said the Brahmin].

Brahmin, there is a sense in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is apagabbha.' For one who has abandoned future lying in a womb and rebirth in a new existence, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, rendered them non-existent, so that they are no longer subject to future arising—I call him 'apagabbha'. Brahmin, the Tathāgata has abandoned future lying in a womb and rebirth in a new existence; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, rendered them non-existent, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. In this sense, Brahmin, one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is apagabbha,' but not in the sense that you mean. (8)

Brahmin, suppose a hen has eight, ten, or twelve eggs. These eggs have been rightly sat upon, rightly warmed, and rightly seasoned by the hen. Which of those chicks, having first broken through the eggshell with the tip of its claw or its beak, would emerge safely? What should it be called—the eldest or the youngest?

'It should be called the eldest, Master Gotama. For it is the eldest among them,' [he replied].

Even so, Brahmin, among a generation submerged in ignorance, born of the egg [of ignorance], and enveloped by the eggshell of ignorance, I alone in the world, having broken through the eggshell of ignorance, have realized the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi). Indeed, Brahmin, I am the eldest and the foremost in the world. Brahmin, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused, my body was calm and unexcited, my mind was concentrated and one-pointed. Then, Brahmin, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion. With the stilling of thought and examination, which brings about internal tranquility and—
22:
—singleness of mind, free from thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of concentration, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna. With the fading away as well of rapture, I dwelt equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experienced happiness with the body; I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily.' With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, pliant, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa). I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion: 'There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere. There too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I reappeared here.' Thus I recollected my manifold past lives in their modes and details.

Brahmin, this was the first knowledge (vijjā) attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute. This, Brahmin, was my first breaking out, like that of a chick from the eggshell. (1)

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, pliant, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings (cutūpapātañāṇa).

With the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing—base and noble, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; I understood how beings fare according to their kamma.
23:
“‘Friends, these beings were endowed with misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. With the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell.’ Or: ‘Friends, these beings were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; they were not revilers of the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views. With the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), which is purified and surpasses that of human beings, I see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and I understand how beings pass on according to their kamma.

“Brahmin, this was the second knowledge (vijjā) attained by me in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance (avijjā) was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute. Brahmin, this was my second breaking out, like that of a chick from the eggshell.

“When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa). I knew as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; I knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I knew as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I knew as it really is: ‘These are the taints (āsava)’; I knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; I knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; I knew as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’ When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), from the taint of existence (bhavāsava), and from the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava). When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ I knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’

“Brahmin, this was the third knowledge (vijjā) attained by me in the last watch of the night. Ignorance (avijjā) was banished and knowledge arose; darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
24:
Darkness was banished and light arose, as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute. Brahmin, this was my third breaking out, like that of a chick from the eggshell.

When this was said, the Brahmin Verañja said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama is the eldest, Master Gotama is the best. Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; in the same way, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka) who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last.”

The First Sutta.

## 2. Sīha Sutta

12. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Gabled Hall. Now at that time, many famous Licchavi princes were sitting together in the assembly hall and were speaking in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma, and in praise of the Saṅgha. At that time, General Sīha, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, was sitting in that assembly. Then it occurred to General Sīha: “Undoubtedly, that Blessed One must be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. For these many famous Licchavi princes, sitting together in the assembly hall, are speaking in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma, and in praise of the Saṅgha. Suppose I were to go to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.” Then General Sīha went to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and said to him: “Venerable sir, I wish to go to see the ascetic Gotama.”

[Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta replied:] “Sīha, why would you, who hold the doctrine of action (kiriyavāda), go to see the ascetic Gotama who holds the doctrine of non-action (akiriyavāda)? For, Sīha, the ascetic Gotama holds the doctrine of non-action; he teaches a Dhamma for the sake of non-action.”
25:
"...and he disciplines his disciples with that doctrine (of non-action)."

Then, General Sīha’s urge to go and see the Blessed One subsided. For a second time, many well-known and famous Licchavis, seated and assembled in the assembly hall, spoke in praise of the Buddha in many ways, spoke in praise of the Dhamma, and spoke in praise of the Saṅgha. For a second time, General Sīha thought: "Undoubtedly, that Blessed One must be the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. For these many well-known and famous Licchavis, seated and assembled in the assembly hall, speak in praise of the Buddha in many ways, speak in praise of the Dhamma, and speak in praise of the Saṅgha. What if I were to approach that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, to see him?"

For a second time, General Sīha approached Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and said to him: "Venerable sir, I wish to approach the ascetic Gotama to see him."

"Sīha, why would you, being a proponent of the doctrine of action (kiriya-vāda), go to see the ascetic Gotama who is a proponent of the doctrine of non-action (akiriya-vāda)? For, Sīha, the ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of non-action, and he disciplines his disciples with that doctrine."

For a second time, General Sīha’s urge to go and see the Blessed One subsided. For a third time, many well-known and famous Licchavis, seated and assembled in the assembly hall, spoke in praise of the Buddha in many ways, spoke in praise of the Dhamma, and spoke in praise of the Saṅgha. For a third time, General Sīha thought: "Undoubtedly, that Blessed One must be the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. For these many well-known and famous Licchavis, seated and assembled in the assembly hall, speak in praise of the Buddha in many ways, speak in praise of the Dhamma, and speak in praise of the Saṅgha. What can these Nigaṇṭhas do to me, whether I ask permission or not? What if I were to approach that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, to see him without asking permission from the Nigaṇṭhas?"

Then, in the afternoon, General Sīha departed from Vesālī with five hundred chariots to see the Blessed One.
26:
He went by vehicle as far as the ground was passable for vehicles, then dismounted and approached the Blessed One on foot. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, General Sīha said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, I have heard this: 'The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action (akiriya-vāda); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of non-action, and he disciplines his disciples with that doctrine.' Venerable sir, do those who say this speak according to the Blessed One's words? Do they not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is not true? Do they explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma? Does no fellow-practitioner, following their speech, have grounds for reproach? For, venerable sir, we do not wish to misrepresent the Blessed One."

"Sīha, there is a way in which one, speaking rightly, could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of non-action, and he disciplines his disciples with that doctrine.' (1)

Sīha, there is a way in which one, speaking rightly, could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of action (kiriya-vāda); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of action, and he disciplines his disciples with that doctrine.' (2)

Sīha, there is a way in which one, speaking rightly, could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of annihilation (uccheda-vāda); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of annihilation, and he disciplines his disciples with that doctrine.' (3)

Sīha, there is a way in which one, speaking rightly, could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is one who is loathsome (jegucchī); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of loathing, and he disciplines his disciples with that doctrine.' (4)

Sīha, there is a way in which one, speaking rightly, could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer (venayiko); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of destruction, and he disciplines his disciples with that doctrine.' (5)

Sīha, there is a way in which one, speaking rightly, could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is an ascetic (tapassī); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of burning away [defilements], and he disciplines his disciples with that doctrine.' (6)"
27:
Sīha, there is a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is free from rebirth; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of freedom from rebirth, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples.' (7)

Sīha, there is a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is one who seeks relief; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of relief, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples.' (8)

Sīha, what is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of non-action (akiriyavāda); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of non-action, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples'?

Sīha, I teach the non-doing of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; I teach the non-doing of many kinds of evil, unwholesome states. Sīha, this is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of non-action (akiriyavāda); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of non-action, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples.' (1)

Sīha, what is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of action (kiriyavāda); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of action, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples'?

Sīha, I teach the doing of bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental conduct; I teach the doing of many kinds of wholesome states. Sīha, this is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of action (kiriyavāda); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of action, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples.' (2)

Sīha, what is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of annihilation (ucchedavāda); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of annihilation, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples'?

Sīha, I teach the annihilation of greed, hatred, and delusion; I teach the annihilation of many kinds of evil, unwholesome states. Sīha, this is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of annihilation (ucchedavāda); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of annihilation, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples.' (3)

Sīha, there is a way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is one who is disgusted; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disgust,
28:
and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples.' What is that way?

Sīha, I am disgusted by bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; I am disgusted by the attainment of many kinds of evil, unwholesome states. Sīha, this is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is one who is disgusted; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of disgust, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples.' (4)

Sīha, what is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer (venayika); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of destruction, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples'?

Sīha, I teach the Dhamma for the destruction of greed, hatred, and delusion; I teach the Dhamma for the destruction of many kinds of evil, unwholesome states. Sīha, this is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer (venayika); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of destruction, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples.' (5)

Sīha, what is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is one who burns away defilements (tapassī); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of burning away defilements, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples'?

Sīha, I say that evil, unwholesome states—bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—are things to be burned away (tapanīya). Sīha, when one has abandoned these evil, unwholesome states that should be burned away, has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, done away with them so that they are no longer subject to future arising, I call such a person one who burns away defilements (tapassī). Sīha, the Tathāgata has abandoned these evil, unwholesome states that should be burned away, has cut them off at the root (ignorance and craving), made them like a palm stump, done away with them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. Sīha, this is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is one who burns away defilements (tapassī); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of burning away defilements, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples.' (6)

Sīha, what is the way in which one speaking rightly could say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is free from rebirth (apagabbha); he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of freedom from rebirth, and with that Dhamma he trains his disciples'?

Sīha, when one has abandoned rebirth and being born again in a future existence, (ignorance and craving)
29:
“I say that one for whom future conception in a womb and rebirth in a new existence are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and are no longer subject to future arising, is ‘free from the womb’ (apagabbho). Sīha, the Tathāgata has abandoned future conception in a womb and rebirth in a new existence; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, done away with them, so that they are no longer subject to future arising. Sīha, it is in this way that one could rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is free from the womb, he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of being free from the womb, and he trains his disciples in that way.’ (7)

Sīha, in what way could one rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama seeks relief (assāsako), he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of relief, and he trains his disciples in that way’? 

Sīha, I seek relief through the supreme relief (of the Path and Fruit); I teach the Dhamma for the sake of relief, and I train my disciples in that way. Sīha, it is in this way that one could rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama seeks relief, he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of relief, and he trains his disciples in that way.’ (8)

When this was said, General Sīha said to the Blessed One: ‘Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante! ... From this day forth, may the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for as long as life lasts.’

‘Sīha, make a thorough investigation. For well-known people like you, it is good to act after thorough investigation,’ the Buddha said.

‘Bhante, by this statement of the Blessed One, I am even more satisfied and delighted. Bhante, if other sectarians had gained me as a disciple, they would have paraded a banner around the whole of Vesālī, saying: “General Sīha has become our disciple.” Yet, the Blessed One tells me: “Sīha, make a thorough investigation. For well-known people like you, it is good to act after thorough investigation.” Bhante, for a second time, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.’

‘Sīha, for a long time your family has been like a well for the Nigaṇṭhas. Therefore, you should consider giving alms to those Nigaṇṭhas when they approach you,’ the Buddha said.”
30:
“‘Bhante, the Blessed One said to me: “Sīha, for a long time your family has been like a well for the Nigaṇṭhas. Therefore, you should consider giving alms to those Nigaṇṭhas when they approach you.” By this statement, I am even more satisfied and delighted with the Blessed One. Bhante, I have heard it said: “The ascetic Gotama says: ‘Gifts should be given only to me, not to others; gifts should be given only to my disciples, not to the disciples of others. Only gifts given to me are of great fruit, not those given to others; only gifts given to my disciples are of great fruit, not those given to the disciples of others.’” Yet, the Blessed One encourages me to give even to the Nigaṇṭhas. Bhante, we shall know the proper time for such giving. Bhante, for a third time, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.’

Then the Blessed One gave General Sīha a gradual instruction (anupubbīkatha). That is to say, he spoke on giving (dāna), on virtue (sīla), and on heaven (sagga); he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the blessings of renunciation. When the Blessed One knew that General Sīha’s mind was ready, softened, free from hindrances, uplifted, and believing, he then revealed the Dhamma teaching unique to the Buddhas (sāmukkaṃsikā dhammadesanā): suffering (dukkha), its origin (samudaya), its cessation (nirodha), and the path (magga).

Just as a clean cloth, free from stains, would properly take the dye, even so, while General Sīha was sitting right there, the stainless, faultless Dhamma-eye (the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry) arose in him: ‘Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.’ Then General Sīha, having seen the Dhamma, reached the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma, having crossed over doubt and become free from wavering, having attained boldness and become independent of others in the Teacher’s teaching, said to the Blessed One: ‘Bhante, may the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, accept my invitation for tomorrow’s meal.’ The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent.

Then General Sīha, having understood the Blessed One’s acceptance, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then General Sīha addressed a certain man: ‘Go, my good man...’”
31:
The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent. Then, General Sīha, understanding the Blessed One's acceptance, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, performed a circumambulation, and departed.

Then, General Sīha addressed a man: "Go, friend, find some meat that is already available (pavattamaṃsa)." Then, at the end of that night, General Sīha, having prepared exquisite hard and soft food in his own residence, had the time announced to the Blessed One: "It is time, Bhante; the meal is ready."

Then, the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, went to the residence of General Sīha and sat down on the prepared seat together with the Saṅgha of monks. At that time, many Nigaṇṭhas were wandering through Vesālī from street to street and from crossroad to crossroad, waving their arms and crying out: "Today, General Sīha has slaughtered a large animal and prepared a meal for the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats that meat killed specifically for him (uddissakata), thus partaking in the bad kamma."

Then, a certain man approached General Sīha and whispered in his ear: "May it please you to know, sir, that many Nigaṇṭhas are wandering through Vesālī from street to street and from crossroad to crossroad, waving their arms and crying out: 'Today, General Sīha has slaughtered a large animal and prepared a meal for the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats that meat killed specifically for him, thus partaking in the bad kamma.'"

"Enough, friend. For a long time, those venerable Nigaṇṭhas have desired to disparage the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Those venerable ones do not cease to falsely, vainly, and untruthfully accuse the Blessed One with what is not real. We would not intentionally deprive a living being of life even for the sake of our own lives."

Then, General Sīha personally served and satisfied the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with exquisite hard and soft food until they were full. When the Blessed One had finished his meal and removed his hand from the bowl, General Sīha sat to one side. As he sat there, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened General Sīha with a Dhamma talk, then rose from his seat and departed. (Second Sutta).
32:
Second Sutta.

## 3. Assājānīya Sutta

13. "Monks, a king's excellent thoroughbred horse endowed with eight qualities is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a factor of royalty. What are the eight? Here, monks, a king's excellent thoroughbred horse (1) is well-born on both sides—from the mother's side and the father's side. He is born in the region (the banks of the Sindhu) where other excellent thoroughbred horses are born. (2) Whatever food is given to him—whether moist or dry—he eats it carefully without scattering it.

(3) He is disgusted by sitting or lying down on his own excrement or urine. (4) He is of pure habits and easy to live with, and does not frighten other horses. (5) Whatever deceit, crookedness like a bull's urine path, crookedness like the letter 'la', or crookedness like a plow handle he has, he reveals it as it really is to the trainer; the trainer then makes an effort to subdue and discipline those faults. (6) He is a carrier of loads; he thinks, 'Whether other horses carry it or not, I alone will carry it in this matter.' (7) When going, he goes only by a straight path. (8) He is strong until the end of his life, and shows his strength. Monks, a king's excellent thoroughbred horse endowed with these eight qualities is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a factor of royalty.

In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with eight qualities is worthy of gifts brought from afar... [pe]... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the eight? Here, monks, a monk (1) is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara), seeing danger in the slightest faults, and training himself in the training rules. (2) Whatever food is given to him—whether coarse or choice—he eats it carefully without being troubled. (3) He is disgusted by bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he is disgusted by falling into various kinds of evil, unwholesome states. (4) He is of pure habits and easy to live with, and does not frighten other monks. (5) Whatever deceit, crookedness like a bull's urine path, crookedness like the letter 'la', or crookedness like a plow handle he has, he reveals it as it really is to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life; the Teacher or the wise companions in the holy life then make an effort to subdue and discipline those faults. (6) He is well-trained (disciplined)..."
33:
“Indeed, whether other bhikkhus train or not, I will train in this matter,” he arouses such a thought. (7) When he goes, he goes only by the straight path. In this context, this is the straight path, namely: right view... right concentration. (8) He dwells with energy aroused, [thinking]: “Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in my body dry up; as long as I have not attained what can be reached by manly strength, manly energy, and manly effort, there shall be no relaxing of energy.” Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these eight qualities is worthy of offerings... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Assakhaḷuṅka Sutta
14. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the eight types of untrained horses and the eight faults of a horse, as well as the eight types of untrained men and the eight faults of a man. Listen and pay close attention; I will speak.”
“Yes, Bhante,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, what are the eight types of untrained horses and the eight faults of a horse?
Bhikkhus, here, a certain untrained horse, when told ‘Go!’ and urged and driven by the charioteer, backs up and turns the chariot backward. Bhikkhus, some untrained horses in this world are of such a nature. Bhikkhus, this is the first fault of a horse.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, here, a certain untrained horse, when told ‘Go!’ and urged and driven by the charioteer, kicks, destroys the wheel rim, and breaks the three-pole frame. Bhikkhus, some untrained horses in this world are of such a nature. Bhikkhus, this is the second fault of a horse.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, here, a certain untrained horse, when told ‘Go!’ and urged and driven by the charioteer, pushes the chariot pole with its thigh and tramples upon the pole itself. Bhikkhus, some untrained horses in this world are of such a nature. Bhikkhus, this is the third fault of a horse.”
34:
“Furthermore, bhikkhus, here, a certain untrained horse, when told ‘Go!’ and urged and driven by the charioteer, takes the wrong path and makes the chariot go off-track. Bhikkhus, some untrained horses in this world are of such a nature. Bhikkhus, this is the fourth fault of a horse.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, here, a certain untrained horse, when told ‘Go!’ and urged and driven by the charioteer, leaps up with its forepart and raises its front legs. Bhikkhus, some untrained horses in this world are of such a nature. Bhikkhus, this is the fifth fault of a horse.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, here, a certain untrained horse, when told ‘Go!’ and urged and driven by the charioteer, without listening to the charioteer and without caring for the goad-stick, bites and destroys the bit with its teeth and goes wherever it pleases. Bhikkhus, some untrained horses in this world are of such a nature. Bhikkhus, this is the sixth fault of a horse.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, here, a certain untrained horse, when told ‘Go!’ and urged and driven by the charioteer, neither goes forward nor backward, but stands still right there like a post. Bhikkhus, some untrained horses in this world are of such a nature. Bhikkhus, this is the seventh fault of a horse.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, here, a certain untrained horse, when told ‘Go!’ and urged and driven by the charioteer, folds its front legs and its back legs and crouches right there, pressing down on all four legs. Bhikkhus, some untrained horses in this world are of such a nature. Bhikkhus, this is the eighth fault of a horse.
Bhikkhus, these are the eight types of untrained horses and the eight faults of a horse.
Bhikkhus, what are the eight types of untrained men and the eight faults of a man?
Bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, bhikkhus accuse a bhikkhu of an offense. That bhikkhu, being accused of an offense by the bhikkhus, evades it by claiming lack of memory, saying ‘I do not remember.’ Bhikkhus, just as that untrained horse, when told ‘Go!’ and urged and driven by the charioteer, backs up and turns the chariot backward; bhikkhus, I say this person is like that untrained horse. Bhikkhus, some untrained men in this world are of such a nature. This, bhikkhus, is the first fault of a man.”
35:
Monks, this is the first fault of a man.

Furthermore, monks, monks accuse a monk of an offense (āpatti). That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, retorts against the accuser: 'What is the use of the talk of an ignorant, incompetent person like you? Do you even think you should speak?' Just as, monks, a bad horse (assakhaḷuṅka), when told 'Go!' and being pricked and urged by the driver, kicks back, strikes the chariot-front, and breaks the triple-pole; even so, monks, I say this person is like that bad horse. Monks, there is such a bad man (purisakhaḷuṅka) in this world. Monks, this is the second fault of a man.

Furthermore, monks, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, counter-accuses the accuser: 'You have fallen into such-and-such an offense; you should first make amends for it.' Just as, monks, a bad horse, when told 'Go!' and being pricked and urged by the driver, pushes against the chariot pole with its thigh and tramples on the pole itself; even so, monks, I say this person is like that bad horse. Monks, there is such a bad man in this world. Monks, this is the third fault of a man.

Furthermore, monks, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, evades the issue with other matters, leads the talk astray, and manifests anger, ill-will, and resentment. Just as, monks, a bad horse, when told 'Go!' and being pricked and urged by the driver, takes a wrong path and makes the chariot go off-road; even so, monks, I say this person is like that bad horse. Monks, there is such a bad man in this world. Monks, this is the fourth fault of a man.

Furthermore, monks, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, throws his arms about in the midst of the Saṅgha. Just as, monks, a bad horse, when told 'Go!' and being pricked and urged by the driver, rears up and lifts its front body and front legs; even so, monks, I say this person is like that bad horse. Monks, there is such a bad man in this world.
36:
Monks, this is the fifth fault of a man.

Furthermore, monks, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, disregarding the Saṅgha and disregarding the accuser, goes wherever he pleases while still having the offense. Just as, monks, a bad horse, when told 'Go!' and being pricked and urged by the driver, disregarding the driver and disregarding the goad, bites through the bit with its teeth and goes wherever it pleases; even so, monks, I say this person is like that bad horse. Monks, there is such a bad man in this world. Monks, this is the sixth fault of a man.

Furthermore, monks, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, thinking 'I have not fallen into an offense, I am not guilty of an offense,' troubles the Saṅgha by remaining silent. Just as, monks, a bad horse, when told 'Go!' and being pricked and urged by the driver, neither moves forward nor backward, but stands right there like a post; even so, monks, I say this person is like that bad horse. Monks, there is such a bad man in this world. Monks, this is the seventh fault of a man.

Furthermore, monks, monks accuse a monk of an offense. That monk, being accused of an offense by the monks, says: 'Venerable sirs, why are you so excessively concerned about me? Right now, I will renounce the training and return to the lower life.' Having renounced the training and returned to the lower life, he says: 'Venerable sirs, are you satisfied now?' Just as, monks, a bad horse, when told 'Go!' and being pricked and urged by the driver, draws in its front legs and draws in its back legs and lies down right there on all four legs; even so, monks, I say this person is like that bad horse. Monks, there is such a bad man in this world. Monks, this is the eighth fault of a man. Monks, these are the eight types of bad men and the eight faults of men.
37:
Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Mala Sutta

15. Bhikkhus, there are these eight stains. What eight?

Bhikkhus, non-recitation is the stain of mantras. Bhikkhus, lack of exertion is the stain of houses.

Bhikkhus, laziness is the stain of beauty. Bhikkhus, heedlessness is the stain of a guard. Bhikkhus, misconduct is the stain of a woman.

Bhikkhus, stinginess is the stain of a giver.

Bhikkhus, evil, unwholesome states are stains in this world and in the next.

Bhikkhus, ignorance is a stain greater than those stains; it is the ultimate stain. Bhikkhus, these are the eight stains.

"Mantras have non-recitation as their stain; houses have lack of exertion as their stain;
Laziness is the stain of beauty; heedlessness is the stain of a guard.
Misconduct is the stain of a woman; stinginess is the stain of a giver;
Evil, unwholesome states are indeed stains in this world and in the next;
Ignorance is a stain greater than those stains; it is the ultimate stain."

Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Dūteyya Sutta

16. Bhikkhus, a monk possessed of eight qualities is fit to go on a mission. What eight? Here, bhikkhus, a monk listens, makes others listen, learns, remembers, understands, makes others understand, is skilled in what is beneficial and what is not, and is not a quarreler. Bhikkhus, a monk possessed of these eight qualities is fit to go on a mission.

Bhikkhus, Sāriputta, possessed of eight qualities, is fit to go on a mission. What eight? Here, bhikkhus, Sāriputta listens, makes others listen, learns, remembers, understands, makes others understand, is skilled in what is beneficial and what is not, and is not a quarreler. Bhikkhus, Sāriputta, possessed of these eight qualities, is fit to go on a mission.

"He who does not waver when reaching an assembly that speaks harshly,
Who does not omit a word, nor hide the message,"
38:
"Nor does he hide the message. He speaks without ambiguity, and does not get angry when questioned;
