## 9. Pahārāda Sutta

19. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Verañjā, at the foot of the Naḷeru Neem tree. Then Pahārāda, lord of the Asuras, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. As Pahārāda, lord of the Asuras, was standing to one side, the Blessed One said to him: "Pahārāda, do the Asuras delight in the great ocean?"
39:
"Venerable Sir, the Asuras delight in the great ocean," (he replied).

"Pahārāda, what are the wonderful and marvelous qualities in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean?" (the Buddha asked).

"Venerable Sir, there are these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean. What are the eight?

Venerable Sir, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves gradually; it does not have an abrupt precipice. Venerable Sir, that the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, and shelves gradually, and does not have an abrupt precipice—this is the first wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the great ocean is stable and does not overstep the shoreline. Venerable Sir, that the great ocean is stable and does not overstep the shoreline—this is the second wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the great ocean does not associate with a dead carcass. If there is a dead carcass in the great ocean, it quickly washes it to the shore and casts it onto dry land. Venerable Sir, that the great ocean does not associate with a dead carcass, and that if there is a dead carcass in the great ocean, it quickly washes it to the shore and casts it onto dry land—this is the third wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, all the great rivers—namely, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī—on reaching the great ocean, give up their former names and clans and are simply called 'the great ocean.' Venerable Sir, that all the great rivers—namely, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī—on reaching the great ocean, give up their former names and clans and are simply called 'the great ocean'—this is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean."
40:
"...seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, although all the streams in the world flow into the great ocean and all the showers of rain fall from the sky, yet neither decrease nor fullness of the great ocean is evident. Venerable Sir, that although all the streams in the world flow into the great ocean and all the showers of rain fall from the sky, yet neither decrease nor fullness of the great ocean is evident—this is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the great ocean has but one taste, the taste of salt. Venerable Sir, that the great ocean has but one taste, the taste of salt—this is the sixth wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the great ocean has many treasures, countless treasures; namely, pearls, gems, beryl, conch, quartz, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and cats-eyes. Venerable Sir, that the great ocean has many treasures, countless treasures—namely, pearls, gems, beryl, conch, quartz, coral, silver, gold, rubies, and cats-eyes—this is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the great ocean is the abode of great beings. These are the beings: the Timi, the Timingala, the Timirapingala, Asuras, Nāgas, and Gandhabbas. There are in the great ocean beings with bodies a hundred yojanas long, two hundred yojanas long, three hundred yojanas long, four hundred yojanas long, and five hundred yojanas long. Venerable Sir, that the great ocean is the abode of great beings—namely, the Timi, the Timingala, the Timirapingala, Asuras, Nāgas, and Gandhabbas—and that there are in the great ocean beings with bodies a hundred yojanas, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, and five hundred yojanas long—this is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean.

Venerable Sir, these are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in the great ocean."
41:
"Seeing these qualities again and again, the Asuras take great delight in the great ocean," (he said). "But, Bhante, do the monks delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'?"

"They do, Pahārāda, the monks delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'," (He replied).

"Bhante, what kind of wonderful and marvelous qualities do the monks see in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation' that they take delight in it?" (he asked).

"Pahārāda, there are eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation', seeing which the monks take great delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'. What are the eight? Just as, Pahārāda, the great ocean is not a sudden precipice at the shore, but has a gradual shelf, a gradual slope, and a gradual inclination; in the same way, Pahārāda, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, there is a gradual training, a gradual performance, and a gradual practice, and there is no sudden penetration of the fruit of Arahantship at the very beginning. Pahārāda, this fact that in this Dhamma-Vinaya there is a gradual training, a gradual performance, and a gradual practice, and no sudden penetration of the fruit of Arahantship at the very beginning, is the first wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'. Seeing this quality again and again, the monks take great delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'.

Furthermore, Pahārāda, just as the great ocean is stable and does not overstep its shore; in the same way, Pahārāda, my disciples do not overstep the training rules I have prescribed for them, even for the sake of their lives. Pahārāda, this fact that my disciples do not overstep the training rules I have prescribed for them even for the sake of their lives is the second wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'. Seeing this quality again and again, the monks take great delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'.

Furthermore, Pahārāda, just as the great ocean does not associate with a foul corpse, and if there is a foul corpse in the great ocean, it quickly washes it to the shore and casts it onto the land; in the same way, Pahārāda, the Sangha does not associate with a person who is immoral, of evil character, of impure and suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions, not a recluse though claiming to be one, not a celibate though claiming to be one, rotten within, lustful, and a heap of filth; having assembled, they quickly expel him. Even if that person is sitting in the midst of the Bhikkhu Sangha, he is indeed far from the Sangha,"
42:
"and the Sangha is far from him. Pahārāda, this fact that the Sangha does not associate with a person who is immoral, of evil character, of impure and suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions, not a recluse though claiming to be one, not a celibate though claiming to be one, rotten within, lustful, and a heap of filth; and that they assemble and quickly expel him, and that even if he sits in the midst of the Sangha, he is far from the Sangha and the Sangha is far from him, is the third wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'. Seeing this wonderful and marvelous quality again and again, the monks take great delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'.

Furthermore, Pahārāda, just as all the great rivers—the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī—on reaching the great ocean, give up their former names and clans and are simply designated as 'the great ocean'; in the same way, Pahārāda, these four castes—Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, and Suddas—having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation' proclaimed by the Tathāgata, give up their former names and clans and are simply designated as 'recluses who are sons of the Sakyan'. Pahārāda, this fact that these four castes—Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, and Suddas—having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation' proclaimed by the Tathāgata, give up their former names and clans and are simply designated as 'recluses who are sons of the Sakyan', is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'. Seeing this quality again and again, the monks take great delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'.

Furthermore, Pahārāda, just as all the large and small rivers in the world flow into the great ocean, and all the streams of rain fall from the sky, yet no decrease or increase in the great ocean is evident because of that; in the same way, Pahārāda, even if many monks attain final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element without residue, no decrease or increase in the Nibbāna-element is evident because of that. Pahārāda, this fact that many monks attain final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna-element without residue, and that no decrease or increase in the Nibbāna-element is evident because of that, is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya 'Dispensation'."
43:
Seeing these qualities again and again, the monks delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya.

“Pahārāda, just as the great ocean has but one taste, the taste of salt; even so, Pahārāda, this Dhamma-Vinaya has but one taste, the taste of liberation (vimutti). Pahārāda, that this Dhamma-Vinaya has but one taste, the taste of liberation, is the sixth wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya, seeing which again and again the monks delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya.

“Pahārāda, just as the great ocean has many treasures, diverse treasures, such as: pearls, gems, beryl, conch, quartz, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and cat’s eye; even so, Pahārāda, this Dhamma-Vinaya has many treasures, diverse treasures, such as: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. Pahārāda, that this Dhamma-Vinaya has many treasures, diverse treasures, such as the four foundations of mindfulness... the noble eightfold path, is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya, seeing which again and again the monks delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya.

“Pahārāda, just as the great ocean is the dwelling place of great beings, such as: the Timi, the Timingala, the Timirapingala, Asuras, Nāgas, and Gandhabbas; and there are in the great ocean beings with bodies a hundred yojanas long, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, four hundred yojanas, and five hundred yojanas long; even so, Pahārāda, this Dhamma-Vinaya is the dwelling place of great beings, such as: the Stream-enterer and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the Once-returner and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; the Non-returner and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; the Arahant and the one practicing for Arahantship. Pahārāda, that this Dhamma-Vinaya is the dwelling place of great beings, such as the Stream-enterer and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the Once-returner and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; the Non-returner and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; the Arahant and the one practicing for Arahantship, is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya, seeing which again and again the monks delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya. These, Pahārāda, are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in this Dhamma-Vinaya."
44:
“Seeing these qualities again and again, the monks delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya,” he said.

Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Uposatha Sutta

20. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the mansion of Migāra’s mother (Visākhā). At that time, the Blessed One was sitting surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks on the Uposatha day. Then the Venerable Ānanda, when the night was far spent, at the end of the first watch, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and with joined palms toward the Blessed One, said: “Venerable Sir, the night is far spent, the first watch has passed. The Saṅgha of monks has been sitting for a long time. Let the Blessed One, Venerable Sir, recite the Pātimokkha to the monks.” When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.

A second time, the Venerable Ānanda, when the night was far spent, at the end of the middle watch, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and with joined palms toward the Blessed One, said: “Venerable Sir, the night is far spent, the middle watch has passed. The Saṅgha of monks has been sitting for a long time. Let the Blessed One, Venerable Sir, recite the Pātimokkha to the monks.” A second time, the Blessed One remained silent.

A third time, the Venerable Ānanda, when the night was far spent, at the end of the last watch, when dawn was rising and the night had a pleasing face, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and with joined palms toward the Blessed One, said: “Venerable Sir, the night is far spent, the last watch has passed. Dawn has risen and the night has a pleasing face. The Saṅgha of monks has been sitting for a long time. Let the Blessed One, Venerable Sir, recite the Pātimokkha to the monks.”

“Ānanda, the assembly is not pure.”

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna thought: “To whom was the Blessed One referring when he said, ‘Ānanda, the assembly is not pure’?” Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna encompassed the whole Saṅgha of monks with his mind and reflected. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna then saw that person who was immoral, of evil character, impure, of suspicious behavior, secretive in his actions, not a recluse though claiming to be one, not a celibate though claiming to be one, rotten within, lustful, and full of filth, sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks. Seeing him, he rose from his seat, approached that person, and said: “Get up, friend! The Blessed One has seen you. You have no communion with the monks.” But that person remained silent.
45:
For the second time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to that person: "Get up, friend! You have been seen by the Blessed One. You have no communion with the bhikkhus." Yet that person remained silent. For the third time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to that person: "Get up, friend! You have been seen by the Blessed One. You have no communion with the bhikkhus." Yet that person remained silent. Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, taking that person by the arm, led him out through the outer gatehouse, bolted the door, and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I have removed that person. The assembly is now pure. May the Blessed One, Venerable Sir, recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus."

"It is wonderful, Moggallāna! It is marvelous, Moggallāna! That this hollow man should wait until he was even taken by the arm!"

Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, from now on you yourselves shall perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha. Bhikkhus, from this day forward, I will not perform the Uposatha nor recite the Pātimokkha. It is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot happen, that a Tathāgata should recite the Pātimokkha in an impure assembly."

"Bhikkhus, there are these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean. What are the eight?

Bhikkhus, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, shelves gradually, and is not an abrupt precipice. Bhikkhus, that the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, shelves gradually, and is not an abrupt precipice—this is the first wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean. ... (to be expanded as before).

Furthermore, bhikkhus, the great ocean is the abode of great beings. In it are these beings: the Timi, the Timiṅgala, the Timirapiṅgala, Asuras, Nāgas, and Gandhabbas. There are in the great ocean individualities even a hundred yojanas long... ... even five hundred yojanas long."
46:
...individualities even five hundred yojanas long—this is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean. These, bhikkhus, are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in the great ocean, seeing which the Asuras delight in the great ocean.

In the same way, bhikkhus, there are eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in this Dhamma-Vinaya, seeing which the bhikkhus delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya. What are the eight?

Just as, bhikkhus, the great ocean slopes gradually, inclines gradually, shelves gradually, and is not an abrupt precipice; in the same way, bhikkhus, in this Dhamma-Vinaya there is gradual training, gradual work, and gradual practice, and there is no sudden penetration of final knowledge. Bhikkhus, that in this Dhamma-Vinaya there is gradual training, gradual work, and gradual practice, and no sudden penetration of final knowledge—this is the first wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya, seeing which the bhikkhus delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya. ...

Just as, bhikkhus, the great ocean is the abode of great beings—the Timi, the Timiṅgala, the Timirapiṅgala, Asuras, Nāgas, and Gandhabbas—and there are individualities even a hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, and five hundred yojanas long; in the same way, bhikkhus, this Dhamma-Vinaya is the abode of great beings. These are the beings: the Stream-enterer and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the Once-returner and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; the Non-returner and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; the Arahant and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship. Bhikkhus, that this Dhamma-Vinaya is the abode of these great beings—the Stream-enterer and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry... ... the Arahant and the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship—this is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality in this Dhamma-Vinaya, seeing which the bhikkhus delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya. These, bhikkhus, are the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities in this Dhamma-Vinaya."

The Tenth (Sutta).
The Second Great Chapter (Mahāvagga).
47:
Seeing these things again and again, the monks take great delight in this Dhamma-Vinaya (the Dispensation).

Tenth Sutta.
The second Mahāvagga is finished.

## 3. Gahapati Vagga
## 1. Paṭhama Ugga Sutta

21. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, at the Gabled Hall. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, you should remember Ugga the householder of Vesālī as being endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities." This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered the monastery.

Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robes, approached the house of Ugga the householder of Vesālī and sat down on the prepared seat. Then Ugga the householder of Vesālī approached that monk, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As Ugga the householder of Vesālī was sitting there, that monk said to him:

"Householder, the Blessed One has declared that you are endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities. What, householder, are those eight wonderful and marvelous qualities with which the Blessed One said you are endowed?"

"Venerable sir, I do not know which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities the Blessed One was referring to when he declared me to be so endowed. However, venerable sir, as for the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities that are found in me, listen to them and attend closely; I will speak."

"Very well, householder," that monk replied to Ugga the householder of Vesālī. Ugga the householder of Vesālī said this:

"Venerable sir, when I first saw the Blessed One from afar, as soon as I saw him, my heart gained confidence in the Blessed One."
48:
Venerable sir, this is the first wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Then, venerable sir, with a confident heart, I attended upon the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave me a progressive discourse, that is to say, a talk on giving, a talk on virtue, and a talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation. When the Blessed One knew that my mind was ready, soft, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, he then revealed the Dhamma teaching special to the Buddhas: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take the dye, even so, while sitting right there, the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose in me: 'Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.'

Venerable sir, having seen the Dhamma, reached the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and fathomed the Dhamma, having crossed over doubt and being free from indecision, having attained boldness and being independent of others in the Teacher's Dispensation, I then and there went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. And I undertook the training rules with celibacy (brahmacariya) as the fifth. Venerable sir, this is the second wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, I had four young wives. Then, venerable sir, I approached those wives and said to them: 'Sisters, I have undertaken the training rules with celibacy as the fifth. Whoever among you wishes may enjoy the wealth and perform merits right here in this house, or you may go to your own relatives' homes. Or if you desire another man, to whom shall I give you?' When I said this, the eldest wife said to me: 'My lord, please give me to such-and-such a man.' Then, venerable sir, I sent for that man, and taking my wife with my left hand and the water vessel with my right hand, I poured the water of dedication for that man. Venerable sir, I do not recall any change in my heart while giving away my young wife. Venerable sir, this is the third wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Furthermore, venerable sir, there is wealth in my family. And that wealth is shared without reservation with those of virtuous and good character. Venerable sir, this is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.
49:
“Venerable sir, when I renounced my young wife, I was not aware of any mental disturbance. Venerable sir, this is the third wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, the wealth in my family home is shared without discrimination with virtuous people of good character. Venerable sir, this is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, whenever I attend to a monk, I do so only with respect, never without respect. Venerable sir, this is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, if that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen only with respect, never without respect. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach him the Dhamma. Venerable sir, this is the sixth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, it is not wonderful that deities approach me and announce, ‘Householder, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One.’ When this is said, venerable sir, I say to those deities, ‘Whether you deities say so or not, the Dhamma is indeed well-expounded by the Blessed One.’ Yet, venerable sir, I do not recall any elation of mind arising from the fact that ‘Deities approach me’ or ‘I converse with deities.’ Venerable sir, this is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, of the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One, I do not see any that are not abandoned in myself. Venerable sir, this is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me. Venerable sir, these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities are found in me. However, I do not know which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities the Blessed One was referring to when he declared me [to be possessed of them].”

Then that monk, having received almsfood at the house of Ugga the householder of Vesālī, rose from his seat and departed. Then, after his meal, when he had returned from his almsround, that monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the monk reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with Ugga the householder of Vesālī.

“Excellent, excellent, monk! Just as Ugga the householder of Vesālī would rightly declare, [he has done so].”
50:
“Monk, I have declared Ugga the householder of Vesālī to be possessed of these very eight wonderful and marvelous qualities. Monk, remember Ugga the householder of Vesālī as being possessed of these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.”

The First Sutta.

## 2 - Second Ugga Sutta

22. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Hatthigāma in the Vajjī country. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, remember Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma as being possessed of eight wonderful and marvelous qualities.” The Blessed One said this, and having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.

Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached the house of Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma and sat down on the prepared seat. Then Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma approached that monk, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma was sitting there, that monk said to him: “Householder, you have been declared by the Blessed One to be possessed of eight wonderful and marvelous qualities. What, householder, are those eight wonderful and marvelous qualities of which you were declared by the Blessed One to be possessed?”

“Venerable sir, I do not know which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities the Blessed One was referring to when he declared me [to be possessed of them]. However, venerable sir, please listen to these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities that are found in me, and attend closely; I will speak.”

“Yes, householder,” that monk replied to Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma. Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma said this: “Venerable sir, while I was enjoying myself in the Nāga forest, I saw the Blessed One from afar for the first time. Upon seeing him, venerable sir, my mind immediately gained confidence in the Blessed One, and my intoxication from liquor vanished. Venerable sir, this is the first wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, with a confident mind, I attended to the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave me a graduated discourse, that is: talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.”
51:
When the Blessed One knew that I had a ready mind, a soft mind, a mind free from hindrances, an uplifted mind, and a confident mind, he revealed the Dhamma teaching special to the Buddhas: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a clean cloth, free of dark stains, would properly take the dye, so too, while sitting right there, the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma—the Path of Stream-entry—arose in me: 'Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.' Venerable sir, I have seen the Dhamma, reached the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma. Having crossed over doubt and being free from hesitation, I have attained confidence in the Teacher’s Dispensation without depending on others. Right there, I went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and I undertook the five precepts with celibacy as the fifth. Venerable sir, this is the second wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, I had four young wives. Then, venerable sir, I went to those wives and said to them: 'Sisters, I have undertaken the five precepts with celibacy as the fifth. Whoever wishes may enjoy the wealth and perform meritorious deeds right here, or she may go to her own relatives' home. Or if you desire another man, to whom shall I give you?' When I said this, venerable sir, the eldest wife said to me: 'Noble sir, please give me to such-and-such a man.' Then, venerable sir, having sent for that man, I took my wife with my left hand and a water-vessel with my right hand, and I poured water over his hand, giving her away. Venerable sir, while giving away my young wife, I do not recall any alteration in my mind. Venerable sir, this is the third wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, there is wealth in my family. That wealth is shared without distinction with those of good character and virtuous conduct. Venerable sir, this is the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, whenever I attend upon a monk, I attend upon him only with respect, not without respect. If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen only with respect, not without respect. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach the Dhamma to him.
52:
Venerable sir, this is the fifth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, when the Saṅgha is invited, deities approach me and announce: 'Householder, such-and-such a monk is one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta); such-and-such is one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta); such-and-such is a body-witness (kāyasakkhī); such-and-such is one attained to vision (diṭṭhippatta); such-and-such is one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta); such-and-such is a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī); such-and-such is a faith-follower (saddhānusārī). Such-and-such a monk is virtuous and of good character; such-and-such is immoral and of evil character.' That they speak thus is not marvelous. Venerable sir, while I am serving the Saṅgha, I do not recall such a thought arising: 'I will give a little to this one, or I will give much to that one.' On the contrary, venerable sir, I give with an impartial mind. Venerable sir, this is the sixth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, deities approach me and announce: 'Householder, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One.' When this is said, venerable sir, I say to those deities: 'Whether you deities say so or not, the Dhamma is indeed well-expounded by the Blessed One.' That I speak thus is not marvelous. Venerable sir, I do not recall any elation of mind because of the fact that deities approach me or that I converse with deities. Venerable sir, this is the seventh wonderful and marvelous quality found in me.

Venerable sir, if I should pass away before the Blessed One, it would not be marvelous if the Blessed One were to declare of me: 'There is no fetter bound by which Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma would return again to this world.' Venerable sir, this is the eighth wonderful and marvelous quality found in me. Venerable sir, these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities are found in me. However, I do not know with which eight wonderful and marvelous qualities the Blessed One declared me to be endowed.

Then that monk, having accepted almsfood at the house of Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed. Then, after his meal, when he had returned from his alms round, that monk went to the Blessed One, bowed, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, he reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma.
53:
"Excellent, excellent, monk! Just as one who wishes to answer rightly should answer, so has Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma answered. Monk, I declare that Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma is endowed with these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities. Monk, remember Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma as being endowed with these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities."

Second Sutta.

## 3 - Paṭhama Hatthaka Sutta

23. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī, at the Aggāḷava Shrine. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as being endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities. What seven? Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is virtuous; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī has a sense of shame; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī has fear of wrongdoing; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is learned; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is generous; monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is wise. Monks, remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as being endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities." The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.

Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached the residence of Hatthaka of Āḷavī and sat down on the prepared seat. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī approached that monk, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. That monk said to Hatthaka of Āḷavī, who was sitting to one side: "Friend, the Blessed One has declared you to be endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.

What seven? 'Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful, virtuous... (p)... has a sense of shame, fear of wrongdoing, is learned, generous, and wise.' Friend, the Blessed One has declared you to be endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities."

"Venerable sir, was there any white-robed layman present there?"

"No, friend, there was no white-robed layman present there."

"It is good, venerable sir, that no white-robed layman was present there."

"Venerable sir, if no white-robed layman was present there..."
54:
"...it is indeed good," he said.

Then that monk, having received almsfood at the house of Hatthaka of Āḷavī, rose from his seat and departed. Then, after the meal, when he had returned from his almsround, that monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: "Venerable sir, in the morning, having dressed and taking my bowl and robe, I approached the residence of Hatthaka of Āḷavī and sat down on the prepared seat. Then, venerable sir, Hatthaka of Āḷavī approached me, paid homage, and sat down to one side. To Hatthaka of Āḷavī, who was sitting there, I said: 'Friend, the Blessed One has declared you to be endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.' What seven? Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful, virtuous... (p)... has a sense of shame, fear of wrongdoing, is learned, generous, and wise. Friend, the Blessed One has declared you to be endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities."

"Venerable sir, when this was said, Hatthaka of Āḷavī said to me: 'Venerable sir, was there any white-robed layman present there?' 'No, friend, there was no white-robed layman present there.' 'It is good, venerable sir, that no white-robed layman was present there. Venerable sir, if no white-robed layman was present there, it is indeed good,' he said."

"Excellent, excellent, monk! That clansman is one of few wishes. He does not wish his existing wholesome qualities to be known by others. Therefore, monk, you should also remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as being endowed with this eighth wonderful and marvelous quality, namely, fewness of wishes."

Third Sutta.

## 4 - Dutiya Hatthaka Sutta

24. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī, at the Aggāḷava Shrine. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, surrounded by about five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. To Hatthaka of Āḷavī, who was sitting there, the Blessed One said: "Hatthaka, your assembly is indeed large. Hatthaka, how do you win over this large assembly?"
55:
"Venerable Sir, I gather this large following by means of the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) taught by the Blessed One. Venerable Sir, when I know, 'This person is to be gathered by giving (dāna),' I gather them by giving. When I know, 'This person is to be gathered by kindly speech (peyyavajja),' I gather them by kindly speech. When I know, 'This person is to be gathered by beneficial conduct (atthacariyā),' I gather them by beneficial conduct. When I know, 'This person is to be gathered by impartiality (samānattatā),' I gather them by impartiality.

Venerable Sir, there is wealth in my family. Just as they do not think that the words of a poor person should be listened to, they do not think the words of one who does not give should be listened to. (However, they think my words should be listened to.)"

"Excellent, excellent, Hatthaka! This method of yours is the right way to gather a large following. Hatthaka, whoever in the past gathered a large following, they all did so by these same four bases of sympathy. Hatthaka, whoever in the future will gather a large following, they all will do so by these same four bases of sympathy. Hatthaka, whoever at present gathers a large following, they all do so by these same four bases of sympathy."

Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, having been shown, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a talk on the Dhamma, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Soon after Hatthaka of Āḷavī had left, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as being endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous qualities. What eight? Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī has faith (saddhā); he is virtuous (sīlavā)... [pe]... he has a sense of shame (hiri); he has fear of wrongdoing (ottappa); he is very learned (bahussuta); he is generous (cāga); he is wise (paññā); and he has fewness of wishes (appiccha). Monks, remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as being endowed with these eight wonderful and marvelous qualities."

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5 - Mahānāma Sutta

25. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in Nigrodha’s Park.
56:
Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, in what way is one a lay follower (upāsaka)?" "Mahānāma, when one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, in that way one is a lay follower."

"Venerable Sir, in what way is a lay follower virtuous?"

"Mahānāma, when a lay follower abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from the use of intoxicating drinks and drugs which cause heedlessness, in that way a lay follower is virtuous."

"Venerable Sir, in what way is a lay follower one who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others?"

"Mahānāma, when a lay follower is himself accomplished in faith but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of faith; when he is himself accomplished in virtue but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of virtue; when he is himself accomplished in generosity but does not encourage others in the accomplishment of generosity; when he himself desires to see the monks but does not encourage others to see the monks; when he himself desires to hear the True Dhamma but does not encourage others to hear the True Dhamma; when he himself retains in mind the teachings he has heard but does not encourage others to retain the teachings in mind; when he himself examines the meaning of the teachings he has heard but does not encourage others to examine the meaning; when he himself, knowing the meaning and knowing the Dhamma, practices in accordance with the Dhamma but does not encourage others to practice in accordance with the Dhamma—in that way, Mahānāma, a lay follower is one who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others."

"Venerable Sir, in what way is a lay follower one who practices for both his own benefit and the benefit of others?"

"Mahānāma, when a lay follower is himself accomplished in faith and encourages others in the accomplishment of faith; when he is himself accomplished in virtue and encourages others in the accomplishment of virtue; when he is himself accomplished in generosity and encourages others in the accomplishment of generosity; when he himself desires to see the monks and encourages others to see the monks; when he himself desires to hear the True Dhamma and encourages others to hear the True Dhamma;"
57:
He himself is one who retains in mind the teachings he has heard, and he encourages others to retain in mind the teachings they have heard. He himself examines the meaning of the teachings he has heard, and he encourages others to examine the meaning of the teachings they have heard. He himself, knowing the meaning and the text, practices in accordance with the Dhamma, and he encourages others to practice in accordance with the Dhamma. It is to this extent, Mahānāma, that a lay follower is practicing for both his own benefit and the benefit of others.

The Fifth Discourse.

## 6 - Jīvaka Sutta

26. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, to what extent is one a lay follower?"

"Jīvaka, when one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, to that extent one is a lay follower."

"But, venerable sir, to what extent is a lay follower virtuous?"

"Jīvaka, when a lay follower abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from wine, liquor, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, to that extent a lay follower is virtuous."

"But, venerable sir, to what extent is a lay follower practicing for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others?"

"Jīvaka, when a lay follower is himself possessed of faith but does not encourage others in the attainment of faith... [and so on]... he himself, knowing the meaning and the text, practices in accordance with the Dhamma, but does not encourage others to practice in accordance with the Dhamma. To this extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others."

"But, venerable sir, to what extent is a lay follower practicing for both his own benefit and the benefit of others?"
58:
Jīvaka, when a lay follower is himself possessed of faith and encourages others in the attainment of faith; he himself is possessed of virtue and encourages others in the attainment of virtue; he himself is possessed of generosity and encourages others in the attainment of generosity; he himself desires to see the monks and encourages others to see the monks; he himself desires to hear the Good Dhamma and encourages others to hear the Good Dhamma; he himself retains in mind the teachings he has heard and encourages others to retain in mind the teachings they have heard; he himself examines the meaning of the teachings he has heard and encourages others to examine the meaning of the teachings they have heard; he himself, knowing the meaning and the text, practices in accordance with the Dhamma and encourages others to practice in accordance with the Dhamma. To this extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for both his own benefit and the benefit of others.

The Sixth Discourse.

## 7 - Paṭhama Bala Sutta

27. Monks, there are these eight powers. Which eight?

Monks, crying is the power of children; anger is the power of women; weapons are the power of thieves; sovereignty is the power of kings; complaining is the power of fools; persuasion is the power of the wise; reflection is the power of the learned; and patience is the power of ascetics and brahmins. Monks, these are the eight powers.

The Seventh Discourse.

## 8 - Dutiya Bala Sutta

28. Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: "Sāriputta, how many are the powers of a monk whose taints are destroyed, possessed of which a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints: 'The taints are destroyed in me'?"

"Venerable sir, there are eight powers of a monk whose taints are destroyed, possessed of which a monk whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints: 'The taints are destroyed in me.' Which eight? Here, venerable sir, a monk whose taints are destroyed has clearly seen all conditioned things as impermanent, as they really are, with correct wisdom. Since a monk whose taints are destroyed has clearly seen all conditioned things as impermanent, as they really are, with correct wisdom, this is a power of a monk whose taints are destroyed, based on which he acknowledges the destruction of the taints: 'The taints are destroyed in me.'" (1)
59:
“Furthermore, bhante, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, sensual pleasures are clearly seen as they really are with right wisdom (insight and path-wisdom) as being like a pit of glowing coals. Since, bhante, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, sensual pleasures are clearly seen as they really are with right wisdom as being like a pit of glowing coals, this is also a strength of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by means of which strength he acknowledges the destruction of taints: ‘Destroyed are my taints.’ (2)

Furthermore, bhante, the mind of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is inclined toward seclusion (Nibbāna), slopes toward seclusion, leans toward seclusion, is established in seclusion, delights in renunciation (the state of a monk), and is entirely detached from things that are the basis for taints. Since, bhante, the mind of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is inclined toward seclusion, slopes toward seclusion, leans toward seclusion, is established in seclusion, delights in renunciation, and is entirely detached from things that are the basis for taints, this is also a strength of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by means of which strength he acknowledges the destruction of taints: ‘Destroyed are my taints.’ (3)

Furthermore, bhante, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed, well-developed. Since, bhante, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed, well-developed, this is also a strength of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by means of which strength he acknowledges the destruction of taints: ‘Destroyed are my taints.’ (4)

Furthermore, bhante, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four bases of power have been developed, well-developed... [Pe] ...the five faculties have been developed, well-developed... [Pe] ...the seven factors of enlightenment have been developed, well-developed... [Pe] ...the Noble Eightfold Path has been developed, well-developed. Since, bhante, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the Noble Eightfold Path has been developed, well-developed, this is also a strength of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by means of which strength he acknowledges the destruction of taints: ‘Destroyed are my taints.’ (5-8)

These, bhante, are the eight strengths of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, endowed with which strengths a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed acknowledges the destruction of taints: ‘Destroyed are my taints.’” (Thus he spoke.)
60:
The Eighth Sutta.

## 9 - Akkhaṇa Sutta

29. “Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling says, ‘The world has its opportunity, the world has its opportunity,’ yet he does not know what is an opportunity and what is not an opportunity. Bhikkhus, there are these eight non-opportunities, wrong times for living the holy life.

What eight? Here, bhikkhus, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Sublime One, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One; and the Dhamma is taught—leading to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to enlightenment, proclaimed by the Sublime One. But this person is born in hell. This, bhikkhus, is the first non-opportunity, the wrong time for living the holy life. (1)

Furthermore, bhikkhus... [Pe] ...the Buddha, the Blessed One; and the Dhamma is taught... But this person is born in the animal realm. [Pe] (2)

Furthermore, bhikkhus... [Pe] ...But this person is born in the realm of hungry ghosts. [Pe] (3)

Furthermore, bhikkhus... [Pe] ...But this person is born in a certain long-lived deva realm (Asaññasatta). [Pe] (4)

Furthermore, bhikkhus... [Pe] ...But this person is born in the remote regions, among the ignorant barbarians, where there is no access for bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, or laywomen. [Pe] (5)

Furthermore, bhikkhus... [Pe] ...But this person is born in the middle country, yet he holds wrong views and has a distorted vision: ‘There is nothing given, nothing sacrificed, nothing offered; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously reborn beings; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who have practiced rightly and are proceeding rightly, who by their own direct knowledge have realized this world and the other world and proclaim them.’ [Pe] (6)

Furthermore, bhikkhus... [Pe] ...But this person is born in the middle country, yet he is unwise, foolish, and mute, unable to understand the meaning of what is well-said and poorly-said. This, bhikkhus, is the seventh non-opportunity, the wrong time for living the holy life.”
61:
(7)
Furthermore, bhikkhus, a Tathāgata has not appeared in the world—an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One... the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. And the Dhamma is not taught—the Dhamma that leads to peace, to unbinding, to enlightenment, as proclaimed by the Sugata. Yet this person is reborn in the middle countries (Majjhima-janapada), and he is wise, not dull, not mute, and is capable of understanding the meaning of what is well-spoken and poorly spoken. This, bhikkhus, is the eighth untimely, inopportune occasion for living the holy life. These, bhikkhus, are the eight untimely, inopportune occasions for living the holy life.

(8)
Bhikkhus, there is only one timely and opportune occasion for living the holy life. What is that one? Here, bhikkhus, a Tathāgata has appeared in the world—an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. And the Dhamma is taught—the Dhamma that leads to peace, to unbinding, to enlightenment, as proclaimed by the Sugata. And this person is reborn in the middle countries, and he is wise, not dull, not mute, and is capable of understanding the meaning of what is well-spoken and poorly spoken. This, bhikkhus, is the one timely and opportune occasion for living the holy life.

(1)
Having obtained the human state when the True Dhamma is well-proclaimed, those who do not seize the moment, they let the moment pass.

Many untimely occasions are spoken of, which are obstacles to the Path. Only occasionally and rarely do Tathāgatas appear in the world.

That ninth moment of a Buddha's arising (Buddhupāda-navama-khana), which is very difficult to obtain in the world, has now arrived. The gain of a human birth and the teaching of the True Dhamma are very difficult to obtain.

In that ninth moment of a Buddha's arising, a person who desires his own welfare should strive to know how to understand the True Dhamma. Indeed, do not let the opportune moment pass. For those who let that ninth moment of a Buddha's arising pass will surely reach hell and grieve.
62:
If one fails in this ninth moment of a Buddha's arising regarding the Ariyan Path, which is called the certainty of the True Dhamma, he will grieve for a long time, like a merchant who has lost his profit. A being obstructed by ignorance, who fails in the True Dhamma, will experience for a long time the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra).

Those who have obtained the human state and have followed the word of the Teacher in the well-proclaimed True Dhamma—whether they followed it in the past, will follow it in the future, or are following it now—and those who practice the Path, the unsurpassed holy life proclaimed by the Buddhas, all of them have penetrated the ninth moment of a Buddha's arising in the world.

The restraint (saṃvara) taught by the One with Vision, the Kinsman of the Sun—in those restraints, one should always be guarded, mindful, and dwell without being soaked (by defilements). In this world, those who have reached the destruction of the taints, they have indeed cut off all underlying tendencies (anusaya) that follow the domain of Māra and have reached the further shore, which is Nibbāna.

Ninth Sutta.

## 10 - Anuruddhamahāvitakka Sutta

30. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira in the Bhesakaḷāvana Deer Park. At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was staying in the Eastern Bamboo Park (Pācīnavaṃsadāya) in the Ceti country. Then, while the Venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: “This Dhamma is for one with few desires, not for one with great desires. This Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent. This Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company. This Dhamma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy. This Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness, not for one with muddled mindfulness. This Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated. This Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.”
63:
“This supramundane Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.” Such was the reflection that arose in his mind. Then the Blessed One, having known the reflection in the mind of the Venerable Anuruddha by his own mind—just as a strong man might extend his folded arm or fold his extended arm—disappeared from the Bhesakaḷāvana Deer Park at Sumsumāragira in the Bhagga country and appeared before the Venerable Anuruddha in the Pācīnavamsadāya in the Ceti country. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. The Venerable Anuruddha, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. As the Venerable Anuruddha was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him:

“Good, good, Anuruddha! It is good, Anuruddha, that you reflect on the thoughts of a Great Man: ‘This supramundane Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desires. This supramundane Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontented. This supramundane Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company. This supramundane Dhamma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy. This supramundane Dhamma is for one who is mindful, not for one who is muddle-minded. This supramundane Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated. This supramundane Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.’ Therefore, Anuruddha, you should also reflect on this eighth thought of a Great Man: ‘This supramundane Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation (nippapañca), who rejoices in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation (papañca), who rejoices in proliferation.’

“Anuruddha, when you reflect on these eight thoughts of a Great Man, then, as much as you desire, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, you will enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion.

“Anuruddha, when you reflect on these eight thoughts of a Great Man, then, as much as you desire, with the subsiding of thought and examination, you will enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and singleness of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration (samādhi).

“Anuruddha, when you reflect on these eight thoughts of a Great Man,”
64:
“Anuruddha, then, as much as you desire, with the fading away of rapture (pīti), you will dwell in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experience happiness (sukha) with the body; you will enter and dwell in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He dwells happily, mindful and with equanimity.’

“Anuruddha, when you reflect on these eight thoughts of a Great Man, then, as much as you desire, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, you will enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

“Anuruddha, when you reflect on these eight thoughts of a Great Man, and you obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, these four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as a chest full of clothes of various colors would appear (delightful) to a householder or a householder's son, even so, to you who dwell content (with the practice of the Great Noble Lineage), your rag-robes (pamsukūla) will appear as something delightful for the sake of enjoyment, for the sake of non-attachment, for the sake of a pleasant dwelling, and for the sake of entering Nibbāna.

“Anuruddha, when you reflect on these eight thoughts of a Great Man, and you obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, these four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as a dish of choice hill-rice, free from black grains, with many soups and curries, would appear (delightful) to a householder or a householder's son, even so, to you who dwell content (with the practice of the Great Noble Lineage), your almsfood gathered by the strength of your legs will appear as something delightful for the sake of enjoyment, for the sake of non-attachment, for the sake of a pleasant dwelling, and for the sake of entering Nibbāna.

“Anuruddha, when you reflect on these eight thoughts of a Great Man, and you obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, these four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as a gabled house, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows closed, would appear (delightful) to a householder or a householder's son, even so, to you who dwell content (with the practice of the Great Noble Lineage), your dwelling at the foot of a tree will appear as something delightful for the sake of enjoyment, for the sake of non-attachment, for the sake of a pleasant dwelling,”
65:
The dwelling at the foot of a tree will appear pleasant to you for the sake of delight, for the sake of being free from distress, for the sake of living in comfort, and for the sake of entering Nibbāna.

Anuruddha, when you reflect upon these eight thoughts of a Great Man, and when you obtain at will, without difficulty or hardship, these four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as a householder or a householder’s son might find pleasure in a couch spread with a long-haired rug, a white woollen coverlet, a variegated woollen coverlet, a rug of kadali-deer hide, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends; even so, for you who live contentedly (with the Great Noble Lineage of contentment regarding lodgings), the bed of grass will appear pleasant for the sake of delight, for the sake of being free from distress, for the sake of living in comfort, and for the sake of entering Nibbāna.

Anuruddha, when you reflect upon these eight thoughts of a Great Man, and when you obtain at will, without difficulty or hardship, these four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, then, Anuruddha, just as a householder or a householder’s son might find pleasure in various medicines—namely, ghee, butter, oil, honey, and molasses; even so, for you who live contentedly (with the Great Noble Lineage of contentment regarding medicinal requisites), the medicine of fermented cow’s urine will appear pleasant for the sake of delight, for the sake of being free from distress, for the sake of living in comfort, and for the sake of entering Nibbāna. Therefore, Anuruddha, you should spend the next rainy season right here in the Eastern Bamboo Grove (Pācīnavaṃsadāya) in the Ceti country."

"Yes, Bhante," the Venerable Anuruddha replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the Venerable Anuruddha with this advice, just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, vanished from the Eastern Bamboo Grove in the Ceti country and appeared in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park, at Suṃsumāragira in the Bhagga country. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, I will teach you the eight thoughts of a Great Man. Listen to that... [pe]... And what, monks, are the eight thoughts of a Great Man?

Monks, this Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desires. Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent. Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company. Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy. Monks, this Dhamma is for one of established mindfulness, not for one of muddled mindfulness. Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated. Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise. Monks, this Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, who rejoices in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who rejoices in proliferation."
66:
Monks, this Dhamma is for one of established mindfulness, not for one of muddled mindfulness. Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated. Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise. Monks, this Dhamma is for one who delights in Nibbāna which is free from proliferation, who rejoices in Nibbāna where there is no proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who rejoices in proliferation.

'Monks, this Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desires'—so it was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, a monk, being of few desires, does not wish: 'May they know me as one of few desires.' Being content, he does not wish: 'May they know me as one who is content.' Being secluded, he does not wish: 'May they know me as one who is secluded.' Being energetic, he does not wish: 'May they know me as one who is energetic.' Having established mindfulness, he does not wish: 'May they know me as one of established mindfulness.' Being concentrated, he does not wish: 'May they know me as one who is concentrated.' Being wise, he does not wish: 'May they know me as one who is wise.' Delighting in Nibbāna which is free from proliferation, he does not wish: 'May they know me as one who delights in Nibbāna which is free from proliferation.' 'Monks, this Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of great desires'—it is with reference to this that this was said. (1)

'Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent'—so it was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, a monk is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the support of the sick. 'Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent'—it is with reference to this that this was said. (2)

'Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company'—so it was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, while a monk is living in seclusion, he is visited by monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians. In such a case, with a mind bent on seclusion, leaning toward seclusion, slanting toward seclusion, established in Nibbāna which is the voidness of conditioned things, and delighting in the state of a recluse, he speaks only such talk as is concerned with dismissing them. 'Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company'—it is with reference to this that this was said. (3)

'Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy'—so it was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, a monk lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states, being steadfast, firm in effort, and not casting off the burden regarding wholesome states.
67:
“‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy.’ Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is strong, firm in exertion, and does not neglect the duty of cultivating wholesome states. ‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is energetic, not for one who is lazy.’ Thus it was said, and it is with reference to this that it was said. (4)

‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who has established mindfulness, not for one who is muddled in mindfulness.’ Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, a monk is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and prudence, one who remembers and recalls what was done and said long ago. ‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who has established mindfulness, not for one who is muddled in mindfulness.’ Thus it was said, and it is with reference to this that it was said. (5)

‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated.’ Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures... [pe]... a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. ‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated.’ Thus it was said, and it is with reference to this that it was said. (6)

‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.’ Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, a monk is wise, possessing wisdom regarding the arising and passing away [of phenomena], which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. ‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.’ Thus it was said, and it is with reference to this that it was said. (7)

‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, who rejoices in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who rejoices in proliferation.’ Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said? Here, monks, the mind of a monk enters into, gains confidence in, settles in, and is liberated in the cessation of proliferation (Nibbāna). ‘Monks, this Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, who rejoices in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who rejoices in proliferation.’ Thus it was said, and it is with reference to this that it was said. (8)

Then the Venerable Anuruddha stayed for the following rains retreat right there in the Eastern Bamboo Park in the Ceti country. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized for himself through direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having reached it, he remained therein.
68:
He understood: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.” And the Venerable Anuruddha became one of the Arahants. Then, having attained Arahantship, the Venerable Anuruddha at that time recited these verses:

“Knowing my thoughts, the Teacher,
Unsurpassed in the world,
Approached me by means of psychic power
With a mind-made body.

Just as my thoughts were,
He taught me even further;
The Buddha, delighting in non-proliferation,
Taught me non-proliferation.

Having understood his Dhamma,
I dwelt delighting in the Teaching;
The three knowledges have been attained,
The Buddha’s bidding has been done.”

Tenth Sutta.
The third chapter, the Gahapati Vagga, is finished.

## 4. Dāna Vagga
## 1. Paṭhama Dāna Sutta
31. “Monks, there are these eight types of giving. What eight? One gives an alms-gift when it comes [on impulse]; one gives out of fear; one gives thinking, ‘He gave to me’; one gives thinking, ‘He will give to me’; one gives thinking, ‘Giving is good’; one gives thinking, ‘I cook, but these do not cook; it is not proper for me who cooks not to give to those who do not cook’; one gives thinking, ‘When I give this gift, a good reputation will spread about me’; one gives for the purpose of adorning the mind and as an equipment for the mind [for Samatha and Vipassanā]. Monks, these are the eight types of giving.”

First Sutta.

## 3. Dānavatthu Sutta

33. "Monks, there are these eight grounds for giving.

What are the eight? One gives a gift out of affection; one gives a gift out of anger; one gives a gift out of delusion; one gives a gift out of fear; one gives a gift, thinking: 'Gifts were given and deeds were done by my father and grandfather before me; it is not proper for me to let this ancient family lineage decline'; one gives a gift, thinking: 'Having given this gift, after the breaking up of the body, after death, I will be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world'; one gives a gift, thinking: 'When I give this gift, my mind becomes clear, and satisfaction and joy arise'; one gives a gift for the purpose of adorning the mind and as a requisite for the mind (for Samatha and Vipassanā). Monks, these are the eight grounds for giving."

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Khetta Sutta

34. "Monks, when seeds are sown in a field endowed with eight qualities, they are not of great fruit, not of great sweetness, and do not thrive. What are the eight qualities? Monks, in this world, the field is uneven; it is stony and pebbly; it is salty; the furrows are not deep; it has no water inlet; it has no water outlet; it has no drain; and it has no embankment. Monks, when seeds are sown in a field endowed with these eight qualities, they are not of great fruit, not of great sweetness, and do not thrive.

In the same way, monks, a gift given to ascetics and brahmins who are endowed with eight qualities is not of great fruit, not of great benefit, not of great splendor, and not of great pervasiveness. What are the eight qualities? Monks, in this world, the ascetics and brahmins have wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. Monks, a gift given to ascetics and brahmins endowed with these eight qualities is not of great fruit, not of great benefit, not of great splendor, and not of great pervasiveness.

Monks, when seeds are sown in a field endowed with eight qualities, they are of great fruit, of great sweetness, and they thrive. What are the eight qualities? Monks, the field is even; it is without stones and pebbles; it is not salty; the furrows are deep; it has a water inlet; it has a water outlet; it has a drain; and it has an embankment. Monks, when seeds are sown in a field endowed with these eight qualities, they are of great fruit, of great sweetness, and they thrive."
70:
In the same way, monks, a gift given to ascetics and brahmins who are endowed with eight qualities is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great pervasiveness. What are the eight qualities? Monks, in this world, the ascetics and brahmins have right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Monks, a gift given to ascetics and brahmins endowed with these eight qualities is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great pervasiveness.

Just as when a field is excellent and the seeds sown are excellent, when the sky provides rain, there is an excellence of grain, an excellence of freedom from pests, an excellence of growth, an excellence of abundance, and an excellence of fruit;

So too, when excellent food is given to ascetics and brahmins of excellent virtue, it brings about fulfillment because that deed performed by the virtuous person is excellent.

Therefore, a person desiring fulfillment, who is himself excellent in this world, should associate with those of excellent wisdom; thus fulfillments are achieved.

Having gained excellence of mind in one accomplished in knowledge (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa), one performs excellence of action and obtains excellence of result.

Knowing the world as it truly is, reaching excellence of vision (vipassanā), and relying on the excellence of the path (sotāpatti-magga), one with a perfected mind reaches the goal (arahatta-phala).

Having shaken off all taints, reaching the excellence of Nibbāna, one is released from all rounds of suffering; that release from all rounds of suffering is called the fulfillment of all.

The Fourth Sutta.

## 7. Sappurisadāna Sutta

37. “Monks, there are these eight gifts of a superior man. What are the eight?

He gives what is clean; he gives what is choice; he gives at the proper time; he gives what is allowable; he gives after investigation; he gives frequently; while giving he settles his mind in confidence; and having given, he is elated. Monks, these are the eight gifts of a superior man.”

At the proper time, he frequently gives a gift—
Clean, choice, and allowable food and drink—
To those who lead the holy life, who are like a good field.

Having relinquished much material wealth, he will have no regret.
Gifts given in this way are praised by the insightful.

Having sacrificed thus, the wise one, endowed with faith,
With a mind of liberation, the learned one is reborn
In a happy world free from suffering.

## 8. Sappurisa Sutta

38. "Monks, when a good person is born into a family, it is for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many people: for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of parents; for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of wife and children; for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of slaves, workers, and servants; for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of friends and colleagues; for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of departed ancestors; for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the king; for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of deities; and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of ascetics and brahmins.

Truly for the benefit of many, the wise one living at home,
Honors his mother and father first, day and night without sloth.

He worships them according to the Dhamma, remembering their past kindness,
And shows respect to those who have gone forth, the homeless ones living the holy life.

Established in faith, a lover of virtue, knowing the teachings, he worships them;
He brings benefit to the king, to the deities, and to his kinsmen and friends.

Well-established in the True Dhamma, he brings benefit to all;
Having removed the stain of stinginess, he goes to the peaceful world.

## 1. Saṅkhittūposatha Sutta

41. Thus have I heard—At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There, the Blessed One addressed the monks, "Monks." "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

Monks, the Uposatha observed with eight factors is of great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great pervasiveness. Monks, how is the Uposatha observed with eight factors of great fruit, great benefit, great radiance, and great pervasiveness?

Monks, in this teaching, a noble disciple reflects thus: "For as long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstain from the destruction of life; they have laid aside the rod, laid aside the sword; they are conscientious and compassionate, dwelling for the welfare of all living beings. For this one night and day, I too will abandon the destruction of life and abstain from the destruction of life; I will be one who has laid aside the rod, laid aside the sword, possessing conscientiousness and compassion, dwelling for the welfare of all living beings. By this factor, I shall imitate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed." He is endowed with this first factor.
