## 2. Vitthatūposatha Sutta

42. Monks, the Uposatha observed in this way, endowed with the eight factors, is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great pervasiveness. How, monks, is the Uposatha observed in this way, endowed with the eight factors, of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great pervasiveness?

Monks, in this teaching, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from taking life; they have laid aside the rod, have laid aside the sword; they are conscientious and compassionate, dwelling for the welfare of all living beings. Today, for this night and day, I too, having abandoned the taking of life, will abstain from taking life; I will be one who has laid aside the rod, laid aside the sword, being conscientious and compassionate, dwelling for the welfare of all living beings. By this factor, I will emulate the Arahants, and I will have observed the Uposatha.' He is endowed with this first factor. ... [pe] ... 'For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned high and luxurious beds, abstain from high and luxurious beds; they sleep on a low bed, either on a small couch or a straw mat. Today, for this night and day, I too, having abandoned high and luxurious beds, will abstain from high and luxurious beds; I will sleep on a low bed, either on a small couch or a straw mat. By this factor, I will emulate the Arahants, and I will have observed the Uposatha.' He is endowed with this eighth factor. Monks, the Uposatha observed in this way, endowed with the eight factors, is of great fruit, of great benefit, of great splendor, and of great pervasiveness.

How great is the fruit, how great the benefit, how great the splendor, and how great the pervasiveness? Monks, just as if someone were to exercise sovereignty and kingship over these sixteen great nations abounding in many treasures—namely, the Aṅgas, Magadhas, Kāsīs, Kosalas, Vajjīs, Mallas, Cetīs, Vaṅgas, Kurus, Pañcālas, Macchas, Sūrasenas, Assakas, Avantis, Gandhāras, and Kambojas—ruling over these sixteen nations is not worth a sixteenth part of the merit of the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors.
82:
Why is that? Monks, compared to celestial bliss, human kingship is like the happiness of a miserable person. Monks, fifty human years are one day and night for the Devas of the Four Great Kings. Thirty of such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. Five hundred such celestial years are the lifespan of the Devas of the Four Great Kings. Monks, it is possible that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Devas of the Four Great Kings. Monks, it was with reference to this that I said: 'Compared to celestial bliss, human kingship is like the happiness of a miserable person.'

Monks, one hundred human years are one day and night for the Tāvatiṃsa Devas. Thirty of such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. One thousand such celestial years are the lifespan of the Tāvatiṃsa Devas. Monks, it is possible that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Tāvatiṃsa Devas. Monks, it was with reference to this that I said: 'Compared to celestial bliss, human kingship is like the happiness of a miserable person.'

Monks, two hundred human years are one day and night for the Yāma Devas. Thirty of such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. Two thousand such celestial years are the lifespan of the Yāma Devas. Monks, it is possible that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Yāma Devas. Monks, it was with reference to this that I said: 'Compared to celestial bliss, human kingship is like the happiness of a miserable person.'

Monks, four hundred human years are one day and night for the Tusita Devas. Thirty of such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. Four thousand such celestial years are the lifespan of the Tusita Devas. Monks, it is possible that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Tusita Devas.
83:
Monks, it is with reference to this that I say: compared to celestial happiness, human kingship is like the happiness of a miserable person. Monks, eight hundred human years are one day and night for the Nimmānarati devas. Thirty such nights make a month, and twelve such months make a year. Eight thousand such celestial years is the lifespan of the Nimmānarati devas. Monks, it is possible that some woman or man here, having observed the eight-factored Uposatha, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Nimmānarati devas. Monks, it is with reference to this that I say: compared to celestial happiness, human kingship is like the happiness of a miserable person.

Monks, sixteen hundred human years are one day and night for the Paranimmitavasavatti devas. Thirty such nights make a month, and twelve such months make a year. Sixteen thousand such celestial years is the lifespan of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas. Monks, it is possible that some woman or man here, having observed the eight-factored Uposatha, after the breaking up of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas. Monks, it is with reference to this that I say: 'Compared to celestial happiness, human kingship is like the happiness of a miserable person.'

One should not kill a living being, nor take what is not given,
One should not speak a lie, nor be a drinker of intoxicants;
One should abstain from unchaste conduct, from sexual intercourse,
One should not eat at night, at the wrong time.

One should not wear garlands nor use perfumes,
One should sleep on a low bed or on a mat spread upon the ground;
This is called the eight-factored Uposatha,
Proclaimed by the Buddha, who has reached the end of suffering.

Both the moon and the sun are beautiful to see,
Shining as far as they revolve;
Dispelling darkness, those travelers of the sky,
They shine in the firmament, illuminating the quarters.
84:
Within the range where those moon and sun revolve, there is wealth such as pearls, gems, fine beryl, Singī gold, and also natural gold; that Singī gold and natural gold are also called jātarūpa and haṭaka. Yet all those treasures, all the moonlight, and the host of stars do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of observing the eight-factored Uposatha. Therefore, a virtuous woman or man should observe the eight-factored Uposatha. Having performed meritorious deeds that yield happiness, being irreproachable, they go to the heavenly state.

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Visākhā Sutta
43. On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra’s mother, Visākhā. Then Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As she was sitting there, the Blessed One said to her:

'Visākhā, when the eight-factored Uposatha is observed, it is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great pervasiveness. And how, Visākhā, is the eight-factored Uposatha observed so that it is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great pervasiveness?

Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple reflects thus: "For as long as they live, the Arahants have abandoned the destruction of life and abstain from it; with clubs and weapons laid aside, they are conscientious and kindly, dwelling compassionate toward all living beings. Today, for this night and day, I too shall abandon the destruction of life and abstain from it; with club and weapon laid aside, I shall be conscientious and kindly, dwelling compassionate toward all living beings. In this factor, I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed." This is the first factor with which it is endowed. ...'
85:
“For as long as they live, the Arahants, having given up high and luxurious beds and seats, refrain from them; they use low beds, either a small couch or a straw mat. Today, for this night and day, I too will give up high and luxurious beds and seats, and refraining from them, I will use a low bed, either a small couch or a straw mat. By this factor, I shall imitate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.” (He reflects thus.) He is endowed with this eighth factor. Visākhā, the Uposatha endowed with these eight factors, when observed in this way, is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great pervasiveness.

How great is the fruit, how great the benefit, how great the splendor, and how great the pervasiveness? Visākhā, suppose someone were to exercise sovereignty and kingship over these sixteen great nations (mahājanapada) abounding in many precious jewels—namely, the Angas, Magadhas, Kāsīs, Kosalans, Vajjīs, Mallas, Cetīs, Vaṅgas, Kurus, Pañcālas, Macchas, Sūrasenas, Assakas, Avantis, Gandhārans, and Kambojas—this is not worth even a sixteenth part of the Uposatha endowed with eight factors. Why is that? Because, Visākhā, human kingship is miserable compared to celestial happiness.

Visākhā, fifty human years are one night and day for the Cātumahārājikā devas. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. Five hundred such celestial years is the lifespan of the Cātumahārājikā devas. It is possible, Visākhā, that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, upon the breakup of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Cātumahārājikā devas. It was with reference to this that I said: ‘Human kingship is miserable compared to celestial happiness.’

Visākhā, one hundred human years are one night and day for the Tāvatiṃsā devas. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. One thousand such celestial years is the lifespan of the Tāvatiṃsā devas. It is possible, Visākhā, that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, upon the breakup of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Tāvatiṃsā devas.
86:
Visākhā, it was with reference to this that I said: ‘Human kingship is miserable compared to celestial happiness.’ Visākhā, two hundred human years... [ellipsis in original]... four hundred human years... [ellipsis in original]... eight hundred human years... [ellipsis in original]... sixteen hundred human years are one night and day for the Paranimmitavasavattī devas. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. Sixteen thousand such celestial years is the lifespan of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas. It is possible, Visākhā, that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with eight factors, upon the breakup of the body, after death, may be reborn in the company of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas. It was with reference to this that I said: ‘Human kingship is miserable compared to celestial happiness.’

One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given,
One should not speak lies, nor be a drinker of intoxicants;
One should abstain from unchaste conduct, from sexual intercourse,
One should not eat at night, at the wrong time.

One should not wear garlands, nor use scents,
One should sleep on a small couch or on a spread upon the ground;
This is called the eightfold Uposatha,
Proclaimed by the Buddha, who has reached the end of suffering.

The moon and the sun, both beautiful to behold,
Shedding light, they revolve as far as they go;
Dispelling darkness, moving through the atmosphere,
They shine in the sky, illuminating the quarters.

Whatever wealth exists within that range—
Pearls, gems, fine beryl,
Singī gold or even mountain gold,
That gold which is called jātarūpa and haṭaka.

Yet these jewels, such as pearls and gems, and all the moonlight...
87:
All the hosts of stars do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the Uposatha observed with the eight factors, just as they cannot match the radiance of the moon.

Therefore, a virtuous woman or man should observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors. Having performed meritorious deeds that result in happiness, being irreproachable, they go to the heavenly realm.

The Third Sutta.

## 4. Vāseṭṭha Sutta

44. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Gabled Hall in the Great Wood. Then the lay follower Vāseṭṭha approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: "Vāseṭṭha, the Uposatha observed with the eight factors is of great fruit. ... (Pe) ... being irreproachable, they go to the heavenly realm."

When this was said, the lay follower Vāseṭṭha said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, if my dear kinsmen and relatives were to observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, it would be for their long-term welfare and happiness. Venerable sir, if all the Khattiyas were to observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, it would be for their long-term welfare and happiness. Venerable sir, if all the Brahmins... the Vessas... the Suddas were to observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, it would be for their long-term welfare and happiness."

"So it is, Vāseṭṭha! So it is, Vāseṭṭha! If all the Khattiyas were to observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, it would be for their long-term welfare and happiness. Vāseṭṭha, if all the Brahmins... the Vessas... the Suddas were to observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, it would be for their long-term welfare and happiness. Vāseṭṭha, if the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and people, were to observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, it would be for the long-term welfare and happiness of the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and people."
88:
"Vāseṭṭha, even if these great Sal trees were to observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, if they had consciousness, it would be for their long-term welfare and happiness. How much more so for one who has become a human being?"

The Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Bojjhā Sutta

45. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇډika's monastery. Then the laywoman Bojjhā approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As she was sitting there, the Blessed One said to her:

"Bojjhā, the Uposatha observed with the eight factors is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great pervasiveness. And how, Bojjhā, is the Uposatha observed with the eight factors of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great pervasiveness?

"Here, Bojjhā, a noble disciple reflects thus: 'For as long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from taking life; with clubs and weapons laid aside, they are conscientious and kindly, dwelling compassionate toward all living beings. For this night and day, I too shall abandon the taking of life and abstain from taking life; with club and weapon laid aside, I shall be conscientious and kindly, dwelling compassionate toward all living beings. In this way, I shall imitate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.' He is endowed with this first factor. ... (Pe) ...

"'For as long as they live, the Arahants, having abandoned high and luxurious beds, abstain from high and luxurious beds; they make their beds low, on a small couch or a straw mat. For this night and day, I too shall abandon high and luxurious beds and abstain from high and luxurious beds; I shall make my bed low, on a small couch or a straw mat. In this way, I shall imitate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.' He is endowed with this eighth factor. Bojjhā, the Uposatha observed in this way with the eight factors is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great pervasiveness. How great is its fruit, its benefit, its splendor, and its pervasiveness?

"Bojjhā, suppose a person were to exercise sovereign power over the sixteen great kingdoms, such as the Angas, which are full of many kinds of precious jewels..."
89:
One might exercise kingship, being the ruler and sovereign over these sixteen nations—namely, the Aṅgas, Magadhas, Kāsīs, Kosalas, Vajjīs, Mallas, Cetīs, Vaṅgas, Kurus, Pañcālas, Macchas, Sūrasenas, Assakas, Avantis, Gandhāras, and Kambojas—yet such kingship over these sixteen nations is not worth even a sixteenth part of the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors. For what reason? Bojjhā, compared to celestial bliss, human kingship is wretched. Bojjhā, fifty human years are a single day and night for the Cātumahārājikā devas. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. Five hundred such celestial years are the lifespan of the Cātumahārājikā devas. It is possible, Bojjhā, that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, might, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of the Cātumahārājikā devas. It was with reference to this that I said: 'Compared to celestial bliss, human kingship is wretched.'

Bojjhā, one hundred human years... [pe]... Bojjhā, two hundred human years... [pe]... four hundred human years... [pe]... eight hundred human years... [pe]... sixteen hundred human years are a single day and night for the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas. Thirty such nights make a month. Twelve such months make a year. Sixteen thousand such celestial years are the lifespan of the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas. It is possible, Bojjhā, that some woman or man here, having observed the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors, might, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas. It was with reference to this that I said: 'Compared to celestial bliss, human kingship is wretched.'

One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given. One should not speak lies, nor be a drinker of intoxicants. One should abstain from unchaste conduct, from sexual intercourse. One should not eat at night, at the wrong time. One should not wear flowers, nor apply scents. One should sleep on a low bed or on a place spread upon the ground. This Uposatha with its eight factors has been shown by the Blessed One who has reached the end of suffering. The moon and the sun, both of them, show things clearly; as far as they shine and glow, revolving in their course,
90:
Dispelling the mass of darkness, those moon and sun moving through the sky, illumining the sky, make the quarters beautiful. Within the range where the moon and sun revolve, there exist such treasures as pearls, gems, fine beryl, Siṅgī gold, and also refined gold, which is called jātarူpa or haṭaka. Yet all those treasures—pearls, gems, and the rest—and all the moonlight and the host of stars, are not worth even a sixteenth part of the merit of observing the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors. Therefore, indeed, a virtuous woman or man should observe the Uposatha endowed with the eight factors. Having performed merits that result in happiness, being blameless, they go to the heavenly state.

The Fifth Sutta.

## 6. Anuruddha Sutta

46. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha had gone for his day-abiding and was in seclusion. Then a number of Manāpakāyikā devatās (deities of the lovely body) approached the Venerable Anuruddha, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those deities said to the Venerable Anuruddha: 'Venerable Anuruddha, we are the deities called Manāpakāyikā. We exercise mastery and control over three things. Venerable Anuruddha, whatever appearance we desire, we obtain that appearance instantly. Whatever voice we desire, we obtain that voice instantly. Whatever happiness we desire, we obtain that happiness instantly. Venerable Anuruddha, we are the deities called Manāpakāyikā; we exercise mastery over these three things.'
91:
‘We can obtain such happiness instantly. Bhante Anuruddha, we are the goddesses named Manāpakāyikā; we exercise authority and power in these three matters.’

Then the thought occurred to Venerable Anuruddha: ‘I wish all these goddesses were blue, blue in color, blue in clothing, and blue in ornaments.’ Then, those goddesses, knowing the thought of Venerable Anuruddha, all became blue, blue in color, blue in clothing, and blue in ornaments.

Then the thought occurred to Venerable Anuruddha: ‘I wish all these goddesses were yellow... [as before]... I wish all these goddesses were red... I wish all these goddesses were white, white in color, white in clothing, and white in ornaments.’ Then, those goddesses, knowing the thought of Venerable Anuruddha, all became white, white in color, white in clothing, and white in ornaments.

Then, one of those goddesses sang, one danced, and one clapped her hands. Just as the sound of a five-piece orchestra, well-tuned, well-practiced, and played by experts, is melodious, enchanting, captivating, endearing, and intoxicating; in the same way, the sound of those goddesses’ ornaments was melodious, enchanting, captivating, endearing, and intoxicating. Then, Venerable Anuruddha lowered his senses.

Then, those goddesses, knowing that ‘Venerable Anuruddha is not enjoying this,’ vanished right there. Then, in the evening, Venerable Anuruddha emerged from his seclusion and approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat to one side. Sitting there, Venerable Anuruddha said this to the Blessed One:

‘Bhante, here I had gone for the day’s abiding and was in seclusion. Then, Bhante, many Manāpakāyikā goddesses approached me. Having approached and paid homage to me, they stood to one side. Standing there, Bhante, those goddesses said this to me: “Bhante Anuruddha, we are the goddesses named Manāpakāyikā; we exercise authority and power in three matters. We can obtain such an appearance instantly; we can obtain such a sound instantly; we can obtain such happiness instantly. Bhante Anuruddha, we are the goddesses named Manāpakāyikā;”’
92:
‘“we exercise authority and power in these three matters. We can obtain it according to our will.” Bhante, then the thought occurred to me: “I wish all these goddesses were blue, blue in color, blue in clothing, and blue in ornaments.” Then, Bhante, those goddesses, knowing my thought, all became blue, blue in color, blue in clothing, and blue in ornaments. Bhante, then this thought occurred to me again: “I wish all these goddesses were yellow... [as before]... I wish all these goddesses were red... I wish all these goddesses were white, white in color, white in clothing, and white in ornaments.” Bhante, then those goddesses, knowing my thought, all became white, white in color, white in clothing, and white in ornaments. Bhante, then one of those goddesses sang, one danced, and one clapped her hands. Just as the sound of a five-piece orchestra, well-tuned, well-practiced, and played by experts, is melodious, enchanting, captivating, endearing, and intoxicating; in the same way, the sound of those goddesses’ ornaments was melodious, enchanting, captivating, endearing, and intoxicating. Bhante, then I lowered my senses. Bhante, then those goddesses, knowing that “Venerable Anuruddha is not enjoying this,” vanished right there. Bhante, with how many qualities should a woman be endowed so that, after the breaking up of the body, after death, she is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyikā goddesses?’

‘Anuruddha, when a woman is endowed with eight qualities, after the breaking up of the body, after death, she is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyikā goddesses. What are the eight? Here, Anuruddha, to whatever husband her parents give her—desiring her welfare, seeking her benefit, out of compassion, and acting out of compassion—she rises before him, sleeps after him, is a willing worker, and behaves pleasingly.’
93: She speaks words that are endearing. (1) She respects, honors, reveres, and venerates those whom her husband respects—whether mother, father, ascetics, or brahmins. She also honors guests who arrive at the home by offering them seats and water. (2) She is skillful and industrious in her husband's household duties, such as working with wool or cotton. She is endowed with the wisdom of means to investigate those tasks, and is capable of performing and organizing them. (3) She knows the work done by the household staff—slaves, messengers, or laborers—as done, and the work not done as not done. She knows the strength or weakness of those who are ill. She distributes the food and snacks to each according to their share. (4) She guards and protects the wealth, grain, gold, or silver that her husband brings home. In regard to those possessions, she is not a spendthrift, not a thief, not a drunkard, and not destructive. (5) She is a lay follower (upāsikā) who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. (6) She is virtuous. She abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from intoxicating drinks and drugs which lead to heedlessness. (7) She is generous. She dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, being open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, one to be asked for help, and delighting in the distribution of alms. (8) "Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these eight qualities, after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas." A husband who always exerts himself with great energy, providing for his wife and children with care...
94:
"A wise and virtuous woman does not despise the husband who provides all her desires and who supports and nurtures her. She does not provoke her husband with jealous or harsh words, and she honors and worships all those whom her husband respects.
She is industrious and not lazy, she manages the domestic staff and attendants with appropriate support, she acts in a way that is pleasing to her husband, and she carefully protects the wealth her husband has accumulated. The woman who acts in this way, following her husband's wishes as described, reaches the realm of the devas known as Manāpakāyika."
Sixth Sutta.
## 7. Dutiya Visākhā Sutta
47. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the mansion of Migāra's mother Visākhā. Then the Blessed One said this to Visākhā, Migāra's mother, who was sitting to one side:
"Visākhā, a woman endowed with eight qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas. What eight?
Here, Visākhā, a woman's parents, desiring her welfare, seeking her benefit, and out of compassion, give her in marriage to a husband. For him, she rises before him, sleeps after him, is willing to do whatever needs to be done, acts pleasingly, and speaks affectionately... [Pe]... she is endowed with generosity. She dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, with hands washed (ready to give), delighting in relinquishment, one to be asked, delighting in sharing and charity. Visākhā, a woman endowed with these eight qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the Manāpakāyika devas."
"The husband who always supports her, constantly striving with great diligence and care, a wise and virtuous woman does not despise that husband who provides all her desires,"
95:
She does not provoke her husband with jealous or harsh words; she honors and respects all those whom her husband respects. Being diligent and not lazy, she supports the servants and attendants appropriately; she acts in a way that pleases her husband and carefully protects the wealth he has accumulated. A woman who conducts herself thus, following her husband's wishes, is reborn among the devas called Manāpakāyika.

Seventh Sutta.

## 8. Nakulamātā Sutta

48. On one occasion, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Sumsumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Wood, the Deer Park. Then Nakulamātā the householder approached the Blessed One... [and sat down]. As she was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to Nakulamātā the householder:

"Nakulamātā, a woman possessed of eight qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the devas called Manāpakāyika. What are the eight?

Here, Nakulamātā, a woman's parents, desiring her welfare, seeking her benefit, out of compassion, give her in marriage to a husband. For him, she rises before him, retires after him, is willing to do whatever needs to be done, acts pleasingly, and speaks affectionately. (1)

She honors, respects, esteems, and reveres those whom her husband respects—whether mother, father, ascetics, or brahmins—and she honors guests with a seat and water. (2)

She is skilled and tireless in her husband's domestic duties, such as wool or cotton work; she is endowed with the ingenuity to investigate the means thereof, and is capable of performing and managing them. (3)

She knows the work done by the internal household of her husband—whether slaves, messengers, or workers—as done, and the work not done as not done. She knows the strength and weakness of those who are ill, and she distributes the food and edibles to each according to their share. (4)

She guards and protects the wealth, grain, silver, and gold that her husband brings home..."
96:
Regarding those possessions, she is not a spendthrift, not a thief, not a drunkard, and not a destroyer. (5)
She is a female lay follower (upāsikā) who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. (6)
She is virtuous; she abstains from taking life... [pe]... she abstains from wine, liquor, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence... [pe]. (7)
She is accomplished in generosity. She dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, one to be asked, and delighting in sharing and almsgiving. (8)
Nakulamātā, a woman possessed of these eight qualities, after the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the devas called Manāpakāyika.

"The husband who always supports her,
Constantly striving and industrious,
That man who provides all her desires,
A wise woman does not despise.

Nor does she provoke her husband
With jealous words or anger;
She honors all those whom her husband respects,
Being a wise woman.

She is industrious and not lazy,
She treats her retinue with kindness,
She acts in ways pleasing to her husband,
And guards the wealth he has gathered.

The woman who conducts herself thus,
Following her husband's will,
Is reborn among the devas called Manāpa,
Where she is destined to go."
The Eighth Sutta.

## 9. Paṭhama Idhalokika Sutta
49. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāramātā Visākhā. Then Visākhā went to the Blessed One... [pe].
As she was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to Visākhā: "Visākhā, a woman possessed of four qualities practices for victory in this world; she has undertaken [the path to] this world."
97:
"She strives for this world. What are the four? Here, Visākhā, a woman is well-organized in her work, she cares for her retinue, she acts in ways pleasing to her husband, and she guards the wealth he has gathered.

And how, Visākhā, is a woman well-organized in her work? Here, Visākhā, whatever the husband's domestic work may be—whether in wool or in cotton—she is skillful and not lazy; she is endowed with an investigating mind as to the means thereof, and is able to do it and manage it. In this way, Visākhā, a woman is well-organized in her work.

And how, Visākhā, does a woman care for her retinue? Here, Visākhā, whatever the husband's domestic retinue may be—whether slaves, messengers, or workers—she knows what has been done by them as done, and what has not been done as not done; she knows the strength and weakness of those who are ill; and she distributes the food, both hard and soft, to each according to their share.

In this way, Visākhā, a woman cares for her retinue. And how, Visākhā, does a woman act in ways pleasing to her husband? Here, Visākhā, whatever is considered unpleasing to the husband, she would not do even for the sake of her life. In this way, Visākhā, a woman acts in ways pleasing to her husband.

And how, Visākhā, does a woman guard the wealth he has gathered? Here, Visākhā, whatever wealth the husband brings home—whether money, grain, silver, or gold—she protects and secures it. Regarding those possessions, she is not a spendthrift, not a thief, not a drunkard, and not a destroyer. In this way, Visākhā, a woman guards the wealth he has gathered. Visākhā, a woman possessed of these four qualities practices for victory in this world; she has undertaken [the path to] this world.

Visākhā, a woman possessed of four qualities practices for victory in the next world; she has undertaken [the path to] the next world. What are the four? Here, Visākhā, a woman is accomplished in faith, accomplished in virtue, accomplished in generosity, and accomplished in wisdom. And how, Visākhā, is a woman accomplished in faith? Here, Visākhā, a woman has faith; she believes in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'The Blessed One is an Arahant because he is worthy of special offerings; he is a Sammāsambuddha because he has correctly realized all things by himself...'"
98:
“Because he is accomplished in knowledge (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa), he is called ‘Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct’ (Vijjācaraṇasampanna). Because he speaks good words, he is called ‘Well-Gone’ (Sugata). Because he knows the world, he is called ‘Knower of the World’ (Lokavidū). Because he is the incomparable leader who tames those who should be tamed, he is called ‘Incomparable Leader of Persons to be Tamed’ (Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi). Because he is the teacher of gods and humans, he is called ‘Teacher of Gods and Humans’ (Satthā Devamanussānaṃ). Because he knows (the Four Noble Truths), he is called ‘The Buddha’. Because he is possessed of great glory, he is called ‘The Blessed One’ (Bhagavā).” (Thus she has faith). In this way, Visākhā, a woman is accomplished in faith.

How, Visākhā, is a woman accomplished in virtue? Here, Visākhā, a woman refrains from killing living beings... [p]... refrains from drinking intoxicants, such as wine and liquor, which cause heedlessness. In this way, Visākhā, a woman is accomplished in virtue.

How, Visākhā, is a woman accomplished in generosity? Here, Visākhā, a woman dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, one to be asked for help, delighting in sharing and giving. In this way, Visākhā, a woman is accomplished in generosity.

How, Visākhā, is a woman accomplished in wisdom? Here, Visākhā, a woman is wise... [p]... In this way, Visākhā, a woman is accomplished in wisdom. Visākhā, a woman endowed with these four qualities practices for victory in the next world; she strives for the next world.

She manages her work well,
Supports her attendants,
Behaves pleasingly to her husband,
And protects what he has earned.

Endowed with faith and virtue,
Kind and free from stinginess,
She always clears the path to welfare
In the future life.

These eight qualities
Are found in a woman;
Such a virtuous woman,
Established in Dhamma and truthful,

Endowed with sixteen aspects,
And possessed of eight factors,
Such a virtuous laywoman,
Is reborn in the delightful heavenly world.
99:
The Ninth Sutta.

## 10. Second Idhalokika Sutta

## 1. Gotamī Sutta
51. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodhārāma (on his first visit). Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said to the Blessed One: “I ask you, Bhante, it would be good if women could receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
“Enough, Gotamī! Do not let the going forth of women from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata be pleasing to you.”
A second time, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said to the Blessed One: “I ask you, Bhante, it would be good if women could receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
“Enough, Gotamī! Do not let the going forth of women from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata be pleasing to you.”
A third time, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said to the Blessed One: “I ask you, Bhante, it would be good if women could receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
“Enough, Gotamī! Do not let the going forth of women from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata be pleasing to you.”
Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, thinking, “The Blessed One does not allow women to receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata,” was sorrowful, sad, with a tearful face and crying, paid homage to the Blessed One, and after showing respect, departed.
102:
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kapilavatthu as long as he liked, set out on a wandering tour toward Vesālī. Wandering by stages, he arrived at Vesālī. There the Blessed One stayed at Vesālī in the Great Wood (Mahāvana) in the Hall with the Peaked Roof (Kūṭāgārasālā). Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, having had her hair cut off and putting on saffron robes, set out for Vesālī with many Sakyan women. In due course, she arrived at the Hall with the Peaked Roof in the Great Wood in Vesālī. Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, with swollen feet and dusty limbs, sorrowful, sad, with a tearful face and crying, stood outside the entrance porch.
The Venerable Ānanda saw Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī standing outside the entrance porch with swollen feet and dusty limbs, sorrowful, sad, with a tearful face and crying. Having seen her, he said: “Gotamī, why are you standing outside the entrance porch with swollen feet and dusty limbs, sorrowful, sad, with a tearful face and crying?”
“It is because, Bhante Ānanda, the Blessed One does not allow women to receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
“Then wait here for a moment, Gotamī, while I ask the Blessed One for the going forth of women from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, he said: “Bhante, this Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is standing outside the entrance porch with swollen feet and dusty limbs, sorrowful, sad, with a tearful face and crying, because the Blessed One does not allow women to receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. I ask you, Bhante, I would like women to receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
“Enough, Ānanda!”
103:
The Blessed One said: "Do not take delight, Ānanda, in the going forth of women from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."

A second time... [pe]... A third time, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I pray, let women receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."

"Enough, Ānanda. Do not take delight in the going forth of women from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."

Then the Venerable Ānanda thought: "The Blessed One does not permit the going forth of women from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata. What if I were to ask the Blessed One for the going forth of women from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata by another way?" Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, is a woman capable, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, of realizing the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arahantship?" "Ānanda, a woman is capable, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, of realizing the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arahantship."

"Venerable Sir, if a woman is capable, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, of realizing the fruit of stream-entry... [pe]... the fruit of arahantship; Venerable Sir, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī has been very helpful to the Blessed One. She is the Blessed One's maternal aunt, his foster-mother, his nurse, the giver of milk. When the Blessed One's mother passed away, she suckled the Blessed One. Venerable Sir, I pray, let women receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata."

"Ānanda, if Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepts eight weighty principles (garudhamma), let that be her full ordination (upasampadā). A bhikkhunī, even if ordained for a hundred years, must perform salutation, rising up, making the añjali gesture, and proper homage toward a bhikkhu ordained that very day. This principle is to be honored, respected, esteemed, and worshiped, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. (1)"
104:
A bhikkhunī must not spend the rains in a residence where there are no bhikkhus. This principle is to be honored, respected, esteemed, and worshiped, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. (2)

Every half-month, a bhikkhunī should expect two things from the Bhikkhu Saṅgha: the asking of the date of the Uposatha and the coming for exhortation. This principle is to be honored, respected, esteemed, and worshiped, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. (3)

After the rains residence, a bhikkhunī must invite (pavāraṇā) before both Saṅghas in respect of three matters: what has been seen, heard, or suspected. This principle is to be honored, respected, esteemed, and worshiped, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. (4)

A bhikkhunī who has committed a grave offense (saṅghādisesa) must undergo the mānatta discipline for a fortnight (pakkhamānatta) before both Saṅghas. This principle is to be honored, respected, esteemed, and worshiped, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. (5)

When a trainee (sikkhamānā) has trained in the six rules for two years, she should seek full ordination from both Saṅghas. This principle is to be honored, respected, esteemed, and worshiped, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. (6)

A bhikkhunī must not in any way revile or abuse a bhikkhu. This principle is to be honored, respected, esteemed, and worshiped, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. (7)

From the day of becoming a monk/nun, the path of speech of bhikkhunīs toward bhikkhus is closed, but the path of speech of bhikkhus toward bhikkhunīs is not closed. This principle is to be honored, respected, esteemed, and worshiped, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. (8)

"Ānanda, if Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepts these eight weighty principles, let that be her full ordination."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having learned these eight weighty principles from the Blessed One, approached Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and said: "Gotamī, if you accept these eight weighty principles, let that be your full ordination—

A bhikkhunī, even if ordained for a hundred years, must perform salutation, rising up, making the añjali gesture, and proper homage toward a bhikkhu ordained that very day,"
105:
This rule too should be revered, respected, esteemed, and honored, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. ...

From the day of ordination, the right of bhikkhunīs to admonish monks is prohibited, but the right of monks to admonish bhikkhunīs is not prohibited. This rule too should be revered, respected, esteemed, and honored, and is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts. Gotamī, if you accept these eight heavy rules (garudhammas), let that acceptance be your full ordination. 

"Venerable Ānanda, just as a young woman or man, fond of ornaments, having washed their head, would receive a garland of lotuses, jasmine, or atimuttaka flowers, and taking it with both hands, would place it on the highest part of the body, the head; even so, Venerable Ānanda, I accept these eight heavy rules, not to be transgressed as long as life lasts," she replied.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī has accepted the eight heavy rules, not to be transgressed as long as life lasts."

"Ānanda, if women had not received the going forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the holy life (brahmacariya) would have lasted long; the true Dhamma (saddhamma) would have remained for a thousand years. But because women have gone forth from the home life into homelessness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, now, Ānanda, the holy life will not last long. Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will remain for only five hundred years.

"Ānanda, just as households with many women and few men are easily assaulted by robbers and thieves; even so, Ānanda, in whatever Dhamma and Vinaya women receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness, that holy life does not last long.

"Ānanda, just as when the disease called 'white rust' (mildew) falls upon a field of ripened rice, that rice field does not last long; even so, Ānanda, in whatever Dhamma and Vinaya women receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness, that holy life does not last long.

"Ānanda, just as when the disease called 'red rot' falls upon a field of ripened sugarcane, that sugarcane field does not last long; even so, Ānanda, in whatever Dhamma and Vinaya women receive the going forth from the home life into homelessness, that holy life does not last long."
106:
That holy life does not last long. Ānanda, just as a man might build an embankment for a great reservoir in advance so that the water does not overflow; even so, Ānanda, I have prescribed in advance these eight heavy rules for bhikkhunīs, not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.

The First Sutta.

## 2. Ovāda Sutta

52. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Woods in the Gabled Hall. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. ... Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, possessed of how many qualities should a monk be appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs?"

"Ānanda, a monk possessed of eight qualities should be appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs. What eight?

"Here, Ānanda, a monk is virtuous... he trains in the rules of training he has undertaken. He is learned... he understands through wisdom. Both Pātimokkhas are handed down to him in detail, well-analyzed, well-mastered, and well-settled, according to the suttas and their phrasing. He is a good speaker, with a good delivery, possessed of urban speech that is clear, distinct, and informative. He is able to instruct, urge, rouse, and gladden the Sangha of bhikkhunīs with a Dhamma talk. He is generally liked and agreeable to the bhikkhunīs. He has never committed a grave offense against a woman who has gone forth in the yellow robe dedicated to the Blessed One.

"He has twenty years of standing or more. Ānanda, a monk possessed of these eight qualities should be appointed as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs."

The Second Sutta.

## 3. Saṅkhitta Sutta

53. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Woods in the Gabled Hall. Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing there, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I ask that the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief..."
107:
"I wish to dwell alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute after hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One," she said. 

"Gotamī, of whatever qualities you may know: 'These qualities lead to passion, not to dispassion; to bondage, not to liberation; to accumulation, not to dispersal; to great desires, not to fewness of desires; to discontent, not to contentment; to socializing, not to seclusion; to laziness, not to arousal of energy; to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support'—you may definitely hold: 'This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher's instruction.'

Gotamī, of whatever qualities you may know: 'These qualities lead to dispassion, not to passion; to liberation, not to bondage; to dispersal, not to accumulation; to fewness of desires, not to great desires; to contentment, not to discontent; to seclusion, not to socializing; to arousal of energy, not to laziness; to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support'—you may definitely hold: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher's instruction,'" (the Blessed One said).

Third Sutta.

## 4. Dīghajāṇu Sutta

54. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Koliyans at a market town of the Koliyans named Kakkarapatta. Then Dīghajāṇu the Koliyan approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, Dīghajāṇu the Koliyan said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, we are laypeople who enjoy sensual pleasures, living in a home crowded with children, using Kāsian sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, and handling gold and silver. Let the Blessed One teach us the Dhamma in a way that will lead to our welfare and happiness in this present life and in the future life."

"Byagghapajja, these four things lead to the welfare and happiness of a clansman in this present life. Which four? Accomplishment of initiative (uṭṭhāna-sampadā), accomplishment of protection (ārakkha-sampadā), good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā), and balanced livelihood (samajīvitā).

And what, Byagghapajja, is the accomplishment of initiative (uṭṭhāna-sampadā)? Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman makes a living by whatever means—whether by farming, trading, cattle-rearing, archery, royal service, or some other craft—"
108:
he is skillful in that work, not lazy; he is endowed with investigative wisdom regarding the means (of that work), and is capable of performing and organizing it. This, Byagghapajja, is called the accomplishment of initiative (uṭṭhāna-sampadā).

And what, Byagghapajja, is the accomplishment of protection (ārakkha-sampadā)? Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman has wealth acquired by energetic initiative, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous and righteously gained. He manages its protection and guarding, thinking: 'How can I ensure that kings do not seize this wealth, thieves do not steal it, fire does not burn it, water does not sweep it away, and unloved heirs do not take it?' This, Byagghapajja, is called the accomplishment of protection (ārakkha-sampadā).

And what, Byagghapajja, is good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā)? Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman dwells in whatever village or market town; in that village or market town, he associates with householders or householders' sons, whether young or old, who are advanced in virtue, endowed with faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom. He stands with them, talks with them, and engages in discussion with them. He emulates the accomplishment of faith in those endowed with faith; he emulates the accomplishment of virtue in those endowed with virtue; he emulates the accomplishment of generosity in those endowed with generosity; he emulates the accomplishment of wisdom in those endowed with wisdom. This, Byagghapajja, is called good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā).

And what, Byagghapajja, is balanced livelihood (samajīvitā)?

Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman, knowing his income and knowing his expenditure, leads a balanced life, neither too extravagant nor too penurious, thinking: 'Thus my income will exceed my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income.' Just as a person with scales or his apprentice, holding up the scales, knows: 'By so much it has dipped, by so much it has risen'; even so, Byagghapajja, a clansman, knowing his income and knowing his expenditure, leads a balanced life, neither too extravagant nor too penurious, thinking: 'Thus my income will exceed my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income.'
109:
Byagghapajja, if this clansman, while having a small income, leads an extravagant life, there are those who will say of him: 'This clansman consumes his wealth like a wood-apple eater.' But, Byagghapajja, if this clansman, while having a large income, leads a wretched life, there are those who will say of him: 'This clansman will die like one who is destitute.' But, Byagghapajja, when a clansman, knowing his income and knowing his expenditure, leads a balanced life, neither too extravagant nor too mean, [thinking]: 'Thus my income will stand exceeding my expenditure, and my expenditure will not stand exceeding my income'—this, Byagghapajja, is called balanced livelihood (samajīvitā).

Byagghapajja, there are these four drains on wealth that has been thus acquired: womanizing, indulgence in intoxicants, indulgence in gambling, and having evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates. Byagghapajja, suppose there were a large reservoir with four inlets and four outlets, and a man were to close the inlets and open the outlets, and the heavens were not to provide adequate rainfall. Byagghapajja, in such a case, only the depletion of that large reservoir is to be expected, not its increase. Even so, Byagghapajja, there are these four drains on wealth that has been thus acquired: womanizing, indulgence in intoxicants, indulgence in gambling, and having evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates.

Byagghapajja, there are these four inlets for wealth that has been thus acquired: not womanizing, not indulging in intoxicants, not indulging in gambling, and having good friends, good companions, and good associates. Byagghapajja, suppose there were a large reservoir with four inlets and four outlets, and a man were to open the inlets and close the outlets, and the heavens were to provide adequate rainfall. Byagghapajja, in such a case, only the increase of that large reservoir is to be expected, not its depletion. Even so, Byagghapajja, there are these four inlets for wealth that has been thus acquired: not womanizing, not indulging in intoxicants, not indulging in gambling, and having good friends, good companions, and good associates. Byagghapajja, these four things lead to the welfare and happiness of a clansman in this very life. Byagghapajja, these four things lead to the welfare and happiness of a clansman in the life to come. What four? The accomplishment of faith (saddhā-sampadā), the accomplishment of virtue (sīla-sampadā), the accomplishment of generosity (cāga-sampadā), and the accomplishment of wisdom (paññā-sampadā).
110:
And what, Byagghapajja, is the accomplishment of faith (saddhā-sampadā)? Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman is faithful; he believes in the Enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'Thus is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened... teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.' This, Byagghapajja, is called the accomplishment of faith.

And what, Byagghapajja, is the accomplishment of virtue (sīla-sampadā)? Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman abstains from the destruction of life... [and] abstains from wines, liquors, and intoxicants that cause heedlessness. This, Byagghapajja, is called the accomplishment of virtue.

And what, Byagghapajja, is the accomplishment of generosity (cāga-sampadā)? Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, one who is responsive to requests, and who delights in the distribution of alms. This, Byagghapajja, is called the accomplishment of generosity.

And what, Byagghapajja, is the accomplishment of wisdom (paññā-sampadā)? Here, Byagghapajja, a clansman is wise; he possesses wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, Byagghapajja, is called the accomplishment of wisdom. These, Byagghapajja, are the four things that lead to the welfare and happiness of a clansman in the life to come.

Energetic in his duties, heedful and organized,
He leads a balanced life and protects his gathered wealth.

Faithful, endowed with virtue, bountiful, and free from stinginess,
He constantly clears the path to welfare in the life to come.

These eight qualities for a faithful householder,
Have been declared by the One named Truth to bring happiness in both worlds:

For welfare in this life and for happiness in the next.
Thus, for the householder, generosity and merit increase.
111:

## 5. Ujjaya Sutta

55. Then the Brahmin Ujjaya approached the Blessed One and exchanged friendly greetings with him. After finishing the exchange of pleasant and memorable words, he sat down at one side. Seated there, the Brahmin Ujjaya said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, we wish to go on a journey. May Master Gotama teach us the Dhamma in such a way that it would be for our welfare and happiness in this present life, and for our welfare and happiness in the future life."

"Brahmin, these four things lead to the welfare and happiness of a man of good family in this present life. What are the four? They are: accomplishment of persistent effort (uṭṭhāna-sampadā), accomplishment of protection (ārakkha-sampadā), good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā), and balanced livelihood (samajīvitā).

And what, Brahmin, is the accomplishment of persistent effort? Here, Brahmin, a man of good family earns his living by whatever means—whether by farming, trade, cattle-rearing, archery, royal service, or any other craft—he is skillful in that work and not lazy. He is endowed with the wisdom of investigating the means thereof, and is capable of performing and organizing it. This, Brahmin, is called the accomplishment of persistent effort.

And what, Brahmin, is the accomplishment of protection? Here, Brahmin, a man of good family possesses wealth acquired by persistent effort, collected by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous and rightfully obtained. He manages to protect and guard that wealth, thinking: 'How can I ensure that kings do not take this wealth, thieves do not take it, fire does not burn it, water does not sweep it away, and unloved heirs do not take it?' This, Brahmin, is called the accomplishment of protection.

And what, Brahmin, is good friendship? Here, Brahmin, in whatever village or town a man of good family dwells, he associates with, converses with, and discusses with householders or householders' sons—whether young but mature in virtue, or old and mature in virtue—who are endowed with faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom. He emulates the accomplishment of faith in those endowed with faith; he emulates the accomplishment of virtue in those endowed with virtue; he emulates the accomplishment of generosity in those endowed with generosity; and he emulates the accomplishment of wisdom in those endowed with wisdom. This, Brahmin, is called good friendship.

And what, Brahmin, is balanced livelihood?
112:
Brahmin, here a man of good family, knowing both the income and expenditure of his wealth, maintains a balanced livelihood, neither too extravagant nor too frugal, thinking: 'In this way, my income will exceed my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income.' Brahmin, just as a weigher or his apprentice, holding the scales, knows: 'By this much it is low, by this much it is high'; even so, Brahmin, a man of good family, knowing both the income and expenditure of his wealth, maintains a balanced livelihood, neither too extravagant nor too frugal, thinking: 'In this way, my income will exceed my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income.'

Brahmin, if this man of good family, having a small income, maintains an extravagant livelihood, there will be those who say of him: 'This man of good family eats his wealth like a wood-apple eater (udumbara-khādī).' But if, Brahmin, this man of good family, having a large income, maintains a miserable livelihood, there will be those who say of him: 'This man of good family will die like a starveling (ajeṭṭhamaraṇa).' But when, Brahmin, a man of good family, knowing both the income and expenditure of his wealth, maintains a balanced livelihood, neither too extravagant nor too frugal, thinking: 'In this way, my income will exceed my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income,' this, Brahmin, is called balanced livelihood.

Brahmin, there are four drains on wealth thus produced: womanizing, addiction to liquor, addiction to gambling, and having evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates. Brahmin, suppose there is a large reservoir with four inlets and four outlets. A man would close the inlets and open the outlets, and the rain would not fall properly. In such a case, Brahmin, only the depletion of that large reservoir is to be expected, not its increase. Even so, Brahmin, there are four drains on wealth thus produced: womanizing, addiction to liquor, addiction to gambling, and having evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates.

Brahmin, there are four sources of increase for wealth thus produced: non-womanizing, non-addiction to liquor, non-addiction to gambling, and having good friends, good companions, and good associates. Brahmin, suppose there is a large reservoir with four inlets and four outlets. A man would open the inlets and close the outlets, and the rain would fall heavily. In such a case, Brahmin, only the increase of that large reservoir is to be expected, not its depletion. Even so, Brahmin, there are four sources of increase for wealth thus produced: non-womanizing,
113:
...not being a womanizer, not being a gambler, and having good friendship. O Brahmin, these four things lead to the welfare and happiness of a clansman in this present life. O Brahmin, these four things lead to the welfare and happiness of a clansman in the future life. What four? Accomplishment of faith, accomplishment of virtue, accomplishment of generosity, and accomplishment of wisdom.

And what, Brahmin, is the accomplishment of faith? Here, Brahmin, a clansman is faithful; he believes in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One: he is an Arahaṃ... [pe]... the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.' This, Brahmin, is called the accomplishment of faith.

And what, Brahmin, is the accomplishment of virtue? Here, Brahmin, a clansman abstains from taking life... [pe]... he abstains from intoxicating drinks and drugs that cause heedlessness. This, Brahmin, is called the accomplishment of virtue.

And what, Brahmin, is the accomplishment of generosity? Here, Brahmin, a clansman dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, and delighting in sharing and giving. This, Brahmin, is called the accomplishment of generosity.

And what, Brahmin, is the accomplishment of wisdom? Here, Brahmin, a clansman is wise... [pe]... he is possessed of noble wisdom that discerns the arising and passing away [of phenomena], which is noble and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, Brahmin, is called the accomplishment of wisdom. O Brahmin, these four things lead to the welfare and happiness of a clansman in the future life.

"Energetic in his duties,
Heedful and organized,
He lives a balanced life,
And protects his gathered wealth.

Faithful, endowed with virtue,
Generous and free from stinginess,
He always clears the path
To safety in the future life.

These eight qualities,
For the faithful householder,
Are declared by the One of True Name
To bring happiness in both worlds.

For welfare in the present life,
And for happiness in the future,
Thus for the householder,
Generosity and merit increase."

The fifth sutta.

## 6 - Bhaya Sutta

56. "Monks, 'peril' is a designation for sensual pleasures. Monks, 'suffering' is a designation for sensual pleasures. Monks, 'disease' is a designation for sensual pleasures. Monks, 'bog' is a designation for sensual pleasures. Monks, 'the womb' is a designation for sensual pleasures.

And why, monks, is 'peril' a designation for sensual pleasures? Because, monks, this being who is infatuated by lust for sensual pleasures and bound by desire and lust is not freed from perils in the present life, nor is he freed from perils in the future life. Therefore, 'peril' is a designation for sensual pleasures. And why, monks, is 'suffering'... [pe]... 'disease'... 'tumor'... 'dart'... 'bond'... 'bog'... Because, monks, this being who is infatuated by lust for sensual pleasures and bound by desire and lust is not freed from the womb in the present life, nor is he freed from the womb in the future life. Therefore, 'the womb' is a designation for sensual pleasures."

"Peril, suffering, disease,
Tumor, dart, and bond,
Bog and the womb—both,
These are called sensual pleasures,
Wherein the worldling is stuck.

Overcome by their pleasant appearance,
He goes again to the womb.
But when a monk is ardent,
And does not neglect clear comprehension,

Such a one, having crossed
This difficult and dangerous path,
Observes the trembling generation,
Subject to birth and old age."

I did not yet know: 'These deities, as a result of this karma, have such food and such experiences of pleasure and pain.' ... [Pe] ... I also knew: 'These deities, as a result of this karma, have such food and such experiences of pleasure and pain.' I did not yet know: 'These deities have such a long life span and such a long duration.' ... [Pe] ... I also knew: 'These deities have such a long life span and such a long duration.' I did not yet know whether I had previously dwelt together with these deities or not. (4-7)

Bhikkhus, it occurred to me: 'If I were to perceive light, see forms, stand with, converse with, and engage in discussion with those deities, and if I were to know of those deities, "These deities are from such and such a heavenly host," and if I were to know, "These deities, as a result of this karma, passed away from that human world and were reborn in this realm," and if I were to know, "These deities have such food and such experiences of pleasure and pain," and if I were to know, "These deities have such a long life span and such a long duration," and if I were to know whether I had previously dwelt together with these deities or not, then this knowledge and vision of mine would be even more purified.'
125:
“Monks, at a later time, while I was dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, I perceived light and saw forms; I stood with, talked to, and engaged in discussion with those deities. I knew those deities: ‘These deities are from such and such a heavenly realm.’ I knew those deities: ‘These deities, having passed away from here, were reborn there as a result of this karma.’ I knew those deities: ‘These deities have such food and such experience of pleasure and pain.’ I knew those deities: ‘These deities have such a long life-span and such a long duration of existence.’ I knew those deities: ‘I have previously lived together with these deities’ or ‘I have not previously lived together with them.’ (8)

Monks, as long as my knowledge and vision regarding the deities, with its eight aspects, was not thoroughly purified, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed supreme enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people. But monks, when my knowledge and vision regarding the deities, with its eight aspects, was thoroughly purified, then I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed supreme enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people. Knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘My liberation of mind is unshakeable; this is my last birth, now there is no more renewed existence.’”

The Fourth Sutta.

## 6 - Vimokkha Sutta

66. “Monks, there are these eight liberations. Which eight? Possessing form, one sees forms. This is the first liberation.

Not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally. This is the second liberation.

One is resolved on the beautiful. This is the third liberation.”
127:
With the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory reaction, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking 'Space is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). This is the fourth liberation (vimokkha).

With the complete transcending of the base of infinite space, thinking 'Consciousness is infinite,' one enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana). This is the fifth liberation (vimokkha).

With the complete transcending of the base of infinite consciousness, thinking 'There is nothing,' one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). This is the sixth liberation (vimokkha).

With the complete transcending of the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). This is the seventh liberation (vimokkha).

With the complete transcending of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha). This is the eighth liberation (vimokkha).

Monks, these are the eight liberations.

Sixth Sutta.

## 10 - Bhūmicāla Sutta

70. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Gabled Hall in the Great Wood. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms. We shall go to the Cāpāla Cetiya for the day's abiding.'

'Yes, Bhante,' the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and taking the sitting mat, he followed closely behind the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One approached the Cāpāla Cetiya and sat down on the prepared seat. The Venerable Ānanda also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. To the Venerable Ānanda, who was sitting to one side,
129:
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, Vesālī is delightful; the Udena Cetiya is delightful; the Gotamaka Cetiya is delightful; the Bahuputtaka Cetiya is delightful; the Sattamba Cetiya is delightful; the Sārandada Cetiya is delightful; the Cāpāla Cetiya is delightful. Ānanda, whosoever has developed, practiced, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken the four bases of psychic power (iddhipāda), could, if he so desired, remain for an aeon (kappa) or for the remainder of an aeon.
