Even though the Blessed One gave such a broad hint and clear sign, the Venerable Ānanda was unable to understand it. (Therefore,) he did not beseech the Blessed One, saying: "Venerable Sir, for the welfare and happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans, may the Blessed One remain for an aeon; may the Sugata remain for an aeon," as if his mind were possessed by Māra. For a second time... (p)... For a third time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, Vesālī is delightful; the Udena Cetiya is delightful; the Gotamaka Cetiya is delightful; the Bahuputtaka Cetiya is delightful; the Sattamba Cetiya is delightful; the Sārandada Cetiya is delightful; the Cāpāla Cetiya is delightful. Ānanda, whosoever has developed, practiced, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken the four bases of psychic power, could, if he so desired, remain for an aeon or for the remainder of an aeon. Ānanda, the Tathāgata has developed, practiced, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken the four bases of psychic power. Therefore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could, if he so desired, remain for an aeon or for the remainder of an aeon."

Even though the Blessed One gave such a broad hint and clear sign, the Venerable Ānanda was unable to understand it. (Therefore,) "Venerable Sir, for the welfare and happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans, may the Blessed One remain for an aeon,
130:
may the Sugata remain for an aeon," he did not beseech the Blessed One, as if his mind were possessed by Māra. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Go, Ānanda, now is the time for you to do as you think fit."

"Very well, Venerable Sir," the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, sat down under a certain tree not far away. Then, not long after the Venerable Ānanda had left, Māra the Evil One addressed the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna; may the Sugata now attain Parinibbāna. Now is the time for the Blessed One's Parinibbāna. Venerable Sir, these words were spoken by the Blessed One: 'O Evil One, I shall not attain Parinibbāna until my monk disciples have become accomplished, disciplined, skilled, attained security from the bonds (yogakkhema), learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing properly, living according to the Dhamma; until they, having learned their own teacher's doctrine, can announce, teach, declare, establish, open, analyze, and make it clear; until they can well-refute the doctrines of others that have arisen, with reason, and teach the marvelous Dhamma.'

Venerable Sir, now the Blessed One's monk disciples are accomplished, disciplined, skilled, have attained security from the bonds, are learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing properly, living according to the Dhamma; they, having learned their own teacher's doctrine, announce, teach, declare, establish, open, analyze, and make it clear; they well-refute the doctrines of others that have arisen, with reason, and teach the marvelous Dhamma.

"Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna; may the Sugata now attain Parinibbāna. Now is the time for the Blessed One's Parinibbāna. Venerable Sir, these words were spoken by the Blessed One: 'O Evil One, I shall not attain Parinibbāna until my nun disciples... (p)... until my laymen disciples... (p)... until my laywomen disciples have become accomplished, disciplined, skilled, attained security from the bonds, learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing properly, living according to the Dhamma; until they, having learned their own teacher's doctrine, can announce, teach, declare, establish, open, analyze, and make it clear; until they can well-refute the doctrines of others that have arisen, with reason, and teach the marvelous Dhamma.'"
131:
"...For that long, I will not pass away," (the Blessed One had previously said).

"Venerable Sir, now the female lay followers (upāsikā) of the Blessed One have become wise, well-trained, and confident. They have reached the safety from the four yokes (Nibbāna). They are learned, upholders of the Dhamma, practitioners of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, practitioners of the proper way, and followers of the Dhamma. Having learned their own teacher's doctrine, they can explain, teach, declare, establish, open, analyze, and make it clear. They can well-refute any arising opposing doctrines with reason and preach the wonderful Dhamma. Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now pass away; let the Sugata pass away. Now is the time for the Blessed One's Parinibbāna."

"Venerable Sir, the Blessed One has indeed spoken these words: 'Evil One, I will not pass away until this holy life (Brahmacariya) of mine—this dispensation—is successful, prosperous, widespread, known by many, well-developed, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans.' Venerable Sir, now the Blessed One's holy life is successful, prosperous, widespread, known by many, well-developed, and well-proclaimed among gods and humans."

"Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now pass away; let the Sugata pass away. Now is the time for the Blessed One's Parinibbāna," he said.

When he said this, the Blessed One said to the Evil Mara: "Mara, do not be concerned. The Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata will take place soon. At the end of three months from today, the Tathāgata will pass away."

Then the Blessed One, while at the Cāpāla Cetiya, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquished the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra). When the life-force was relinquished by the Blessed One, a great, terrifying, and hair-raising earthquake occurred, and celestial drums thundered. Then the Blessed One, understanding this matter, uttered this inspired utterance (Udāna) at that time:

"The Sage, weighing the incomparable Nibbāna and the process of repeated existence, has relinquished the karma that constructs existence. Delighting in the internal (meditation) and well-concentrated, he has broken the net of defilements like a coat of mail."
132:
Delighting in the internal (meditation) and well-concentrated, he has broken the net of defilements like a coat of mail."

Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: "How wonderful, how marvelous! This earthquake is indeed great; this earthquake is indeed very great, terrifying, and hair-raising. Celestial drums also thundered. What is the cause, what is the condition for the appearance of this great earthquake?"

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down at one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "How wonderful, Venerable Sir, how marvelous, Venerable Sir! This earthquake is indeed great; this earthquake is indeed very great, terrifying, and hair-raising. Celestial drums also thundered. Venerable Sir, what is the cause, what is the condition for the appearance of this great earthquake?"

"Ānanda, there are these eight causes and eight conditions for the appearance of a great earthquake. What eight? Ānanda, this great earth is established on water, the water is established on wind, and the wind is established in space. Ānanda, there is a time when great winds blow; when the great winds blow, they move the water; when the water is moved, it moves the earth. This, Ānanda, is the first cause and the first condition for the appearance of a great earthquake. (1)

Furthermore, Ānanda, an ascetic (samaṇa) or a brahmin who possesses psychic power and has attained mastery over the mind, or a deity of great power and majesty, has developed a limited perception of earth and an immeasurable perception of water. He makes this earth shake, tremble, quake, and rock. This, Ānanda, is the second cause and the second condition for the appearance of a great earthquake. (2)

Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Bodhisatta, mindful and clearly comprehending, passes away from the Tusita heaven and descends into his mother's womb, then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and rocks. This, Ānanda, is the third cause and the third condition for the appearance of a great earthquake. (3)

Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Bodhisatta, mindful and clearly comprehending, comes out of his mother's womb, then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and rocks. This, Ānanda, is the fourth cause and the fourth condition for the appearance of a great earthquake. (4)

Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata attains the supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), then this earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and rocks."
133:
This is the fifth cause and condition for the occurrence of a great earthquake. (5)

Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata sets in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, this great earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and quivers. This is the sixth cause and condition for the occurrence of a great earthquake. (6)

Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata, mindful and clearly comprehending, relinquishes the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), this great earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and quivers. This is the seventh cause and condition for the occurrence of a great earthquake. (7)

Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata attains final Nibbāna in the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), this great earth shakes, trembles, quakes, and quivers. This is the eighth cause and condition for the occurrence of a great earthquake. (8)

Ānanda, these are the eight causes and conditions for the occurrence of a great earthquake.

Tenth Sutta.

The second chapter, the Bhūmicāla Vagga, is finished.

## 3. First Discourse on Mindfulness of Death

73. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Nātika in the Brick House. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks." "Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, mindfulness of death, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and benefit; it merges into the Deathless and ends in the Deathless. Monks, you should develop mindfulness of death."

When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death." "But how, monk, do you develop mindfulness of death?"
136:
"Venerable Sir, it occurs to me: 'Oh, that I might live for a day and a night, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death." (1)

Another monk also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death." "But how, monk, do you develop mindfulness of death?"

"Venerable Sir, it occurs to me: 'Oh, that I might live for a day, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death." (2)

Another monk also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death." "But how, monk, do you develop mindfulness of death?"

"Venerable Sir, it occurs to me: 'Oh, that I might live for half a day, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death." (3)

Another monk also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death." "But how, monk, do you develop mindfulness of death?"

"Venerable Sir, it occurs to me: 'Oh, that I might live for the time it takes to eat one meal of almsfood, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death." (4)

Another monk also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death." "But how, monk, do you develop mindfulness of death?"

"Venerable Sir, it occurs to me: 'Oh, that I might live for the time it takes to eat half a meal of almsfood, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching; much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death." (5)

Another monk also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death."
137:
"Bhikkhu, how do you develop mindfulness of death?" (He asked).

"Venerable Sir, it occurs to me: 'O, that I might live for the duration it takes to chew and swallow four or five mouthfuls of food; I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching, much indeed would be done by me (in the monk's task).' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death." (He replied). (6)

Another bhikkhu also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death." "Bhikkhu, how do you develop mindfulness of death?" (He asked).

"Venerable Sir, it occurs to me: 'O, that I might live for the duration it takes to chew and swallow one mouthful of food; I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching, much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death." (He replied). (7)

Another bhikkhu also said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I too develop mindfulness of death." "Bhikkhu, how do you develop mindfulness of death?" (He asked).

"Venerable Sir, it occurs to me: 'O, that I might live for the duration it takes to breathe in and breathe out, or to breathe out and breathe in; I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching, much indeed would be done by me.' In this way, Venerable Sir, I develop mindfulness of death." (He replied). (8)

When this was said, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus:

"Bhikkhus, the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'O, that I might live for a day and a night, I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching, much indeed would be done by me'; and the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'O, that I might live for a day...'; and the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'O, that I might live for half a day...'; and the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'O, that I might live for the duration of one meal...'; and the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'O, that I might live for the duration of half a meal...'
138:
...and the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'O, that I might live for the duration it takes to chew and swallow four or five mouthfuls of food; I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching, much indeed would be done by me'—these, bhikkhus, are called bhikkhus who dwell negligent, who develop mindfulness of death sluggishly for the destruction of the taints.

But, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'O, that I might live for the duration it takes to chew and swallow one mouthful of food; I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching, much indeed would be done by me'; and the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death in this way: 'O, that I might live for the duration it takes to breathe in and breathe out, or to breathe out and breathe in; I would attend to the Blessed One's teaching, much indeed would be done by me'—these, bhikkhus, are called bhikkhus who dwell diligent, who develop mindfulness of death keenly for the destruction of the taints.

Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: 'We will dwell diligent; we will develop mindfulness of death keenly for the destruction of the taints.' Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves."

## 4. Dutiya Maraṇassati Sutta

74. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nātika in the Brick House. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: ... "Bhikkhus, mindfulness of death, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the Deathless and has the Deathless as its consummation. And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of death developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit, plunges into the Deathless, and has the Deathless as its consummation?

Here, bhikkhus, as the day passes and night arrives, a bhikkhu reflects thus: 'Many are the causes of my death. A snake might bite me, or a scorpion might sting me, or a centipede might sting me; because of that I might die. That would be an obstacle for me. Or I might stumble and fall, or the food I have eaten might disagree with me and become corrupted, or my bile might be provoked, or my phlegm might be provoked, or sharp winds might cut through me;'
139: "Humans might attack me, or non-humans might attack me; because of that, I might die. That would be an obstacle for me." Thus he reflects. Monks, that monk should reflect: "Are there any evil, unwholesome states unabandoned in me that would be an obstacle for me if I were to die during the night?" Monks, if while reflecting, the monk knows: "There are evil, unwholesome states unabandoned in me that would be an obstacle for me if I were to die during the night," then, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, endeavor, striving, unrelentingness, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very evil, unwholesome states. Just as, monks, a person whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire would apply extraordinary desire, effort, endeavor, striving, unrelentingness, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish the fire on his clothes or head; even so, monks, that monk should apply extraordinary desire, effort, endeavor, striving, unrelentingness, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very evil, unwholesome states. If, however, monks, while reflecting, the monk knows: "There are no evil, unwholesome states unabandoned in me that would be an obstacle for me if I were to die during the night," then, monks, that monk should dwell with joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states. Furthermore, monks, in this Dispensation, a monk, when the night has passed and the day has arisen, reflects thus: "Many are the causes of my death—a snake might bite me, a scorpion might sting me, or a centipede might bite me; because of that, I might die. That would be an obstacle for me. I might stumble and fall, or the food I have eaten might disagree with me, or my bile might be disturbed, or my phlegm might be disturbed, or sharp winds might cut through me. Humans might attack me, or non-humans might attack me; because of that, I might die. That would be an obstacle for me." Monks, that monk should reflect: "Are there any evil, unwholesome states unabandoned in me that would be an obstacle for me if I were to die during the day?"
140:
Monks, if a monk, while reflecting, knows thus: 'There are within me evil unwholesome states not yet abandoned which would be an obstacle to me if I were to die during the day,' then, monks, that monk should apply extreme desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to abandon those evil unwholesome states.

Monks, just as a person whose clothes or head are on fire would apply extreme desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to extinguish the fire on his clothes or head; even so, monks, that monk should apply extreme desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to abandon those evil unwholesome states.

But monks, if a monk, while reflecting, knows thus: 'There are no evil unwholesome states within me not yet abandoned which would be an obstacle to me if I were to die during the day,' then, monks, that monk should dwell with that very joy and gladness (pīti-pāmojja), training day and night in wholesome states.

Monks, when mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) is thus developed and cultivated, it is of great fruit and great benefit; it merges into the Deathless (Nibbāna) and has the Deathless as its consummation.

Fourth Sutta.

## 5. Paṭhama Sampadā Sutta

Possessed of faith and virtue, generous and free from stinginess, he constantly clears the path to welfare in the future life. ## 6. Second Sampadā Sutta
76. Monks, there are these eight accomplishments (sampadā). What eight? The accomplishment of diligence (uṭṭhānasampadā), the accomplishment of protection (ārakkhasampadā), good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā), balanced living (samajīvitā), the accomplishment of faith (saddhāsampadā), the accomplishment of virtue (sīlasampadā), the accomplishment of generosity (cāgasampadā), and the accomplishment of wisdom (paññāsampadā).

And what, monks, is the accomplishment of diligence? Here, monks, a clansman earns his living by whatever means—whether by farming, trade, cattle-breeding, archery, royal service, or some other craft—he is skillful in that work and not lazy; he is endowed with the ability to investigate the means [to success in that work], and is capable of acting and organizing. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of diligence.

And what, monks, is the accomplishment of protection? Here, monks, a clansman possesses wealth acquired by energetic effort, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained. He manages to protect and guard it, thinking: 'How can I ensure that kings do not seize my wealth, thieves do not steal it, fire does not burn it, water does not sweep it away, and hateful heirs do not take it?' This, monks, is called the accomplishment of protection.

And what, monks, is good friendship? Here, monks, in whatever village or town a clansman dwells, he associates with, converses with, and engages in discussion with householders or householders' sons—whether young and mature in virtue, or old and mature in virtue—who are accomplished in faith, virtue, generosity, and wisdom. He emulates the accomplishment of faith in those accomplished in faith; he emulates the accomplishment of virtue in those accomplished in virtue; he emulates the accomplishment of generosity in those accomplished in generosity; and he emulates the accomplishment of wisdom in those accomplished in wisdom. This, monks, is called good friendship.

And what, monks, is balanced living? Here, monks, a clansman, knowing his income and knowing his expenditure, leads a balanced life, neither too extravagant nor too penurious, [thinking]: 'Thus my income will exceed my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income.' Just as, monks, a scale-holder or his apprentice, holding up a scale, knows: 'By so much it has dipped, by so much it has risen'; even so, monks, a clansman, knowing his income and knowing his expenditure, leads a balanced life, neither too extravagant nor too penurious, [thinking]: 'Thus my income will exceed my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income.'

Monks, if this clansman, while having a small income, leads an extravagant life, there would be those who say of him: 'This clansman eats his wealth like a wood-apple eater.'
142:
Monks, if this clansman, while having a large income, leads a penurious life, there would be those who say of him: 'This clansman will die a starveling's death (without support).' But when, monks, a clansman, knowing his income and knowing his expenditure, leads a balanced life, neither too extravagant nor too penurious, [thinking]: 'Thus my income will exceed my expenditure, and my expenditure will not exceed my income,' this, monks, is called balanced living.

And what, monks, is the accomplishment of faith? Here, monks, a clansman has faith; he believes in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: 'The Blessed One is such because he is an Arahant... [as before]... Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.' This, monks, is called the accomplishment of faith.

And what, monks, is the accomplishment of virtue? Here, monks, a clansman abstains from the destruction of life... [as before]... abstains from the use of intoxicants, wines, and liquors, which are the basis for negligence. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of virtue.

And what, monks, is the accomplishment of generosity? Here, monks, a clansman... [as before]... dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, devoted to charity, delighting in giving and sharing, one to be asked for help. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of generosity.

And what, monks, is the accomplishment of wisdom? Here, monks, a clansman is wise... [as before]... possessed of noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called the accomplishment of wisdom. These, monks, are the eight accomplishments.

[Verses:]
Diligence in his spheres of work,
Heedful and possessing management,
He leads a balanced life,
And guards the wealth he has amassed.

Faithful, accomplished in virtue,
Generous, free from stinginess,
He constantly clears the path
To well-being in the future life.

Thus these eight qualities
For a faithful seeker of a home,
Are declared by the One of True Name
To bring happiness in both worlds.

For the welfare and benefit in this life,
And for happiness in the life to come,
Thus for a householder, generosity
And other merits increase.

## 1. Satisampajañña Sutta

81. Monks, when there is no mindfulness and clear comprehension, for one who lacks mindfulness and clear comprehension, the proximate cause for moral shame and moral dread is destroyed. When there is no moral shame and moral dread, for one who lacks moral shame and moral dread, the proximate cause for sense restraint is destroyed. When there is no sense restraint, for one who lacks sense restraint, the proximate cause for virtue is destroyed.
151:
When virtue is absent, for one who is deficient in virtue, right concentration (sammā-samādhi) lacks its proximate cause. When right concentration is absent, for one who is deficient in right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana) lacks its proximate cause. When the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is absent, for one who is deficient in the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the knowledge of disenchantment (nibbidā) and the knowledge of dispassion (virāga - path knowledge) lack their proximate cause. When the knowledge of disenchantment and dispassion are absent, for one who is deficient in the knowledge of disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana - the vision of reviewing knowledge that knows liberation from defilements) lacks its proximate cause.

Bhikkhus, just as when a tree is deficient in branches and foliage, its sprouts do not reach fulfillment, nor do its bark, softwood, or heartwood; in the same way, bhikkhus, when mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) are absent, for one who is deficient in mindfulness and clear comprehension, shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) lack their proximate cause. When shame and fear of wrongdoing are absent, for one who is deficient in shame and fear of wrongdoing, restraint of the faculties (indriya-saṃvara) lacks its proximate cause. ... Bhikkhus, when mindfulness and clear comprehension are present, for one who is possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, shame and fear of wrongdoing possess their proximate cause. When shame and fear of wrongdoing are present, for one who is possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing, restraint of the faculties possesses its proximate cause. When restraint of the faculties is present, for one who is possessed of restraint of the faculties, virtue (sīla) possesses its proximate cause. When virtue is present, for one who is possessed of virtue, right concentration possesses its proximate cause. When right concentration is present, for one who is possessed of right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are possesses its proximate cause. When the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is present, for one who is possessed of the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the knowledge of disenchantment and dispassion possesses its proximate cause. When the knowledge of disenchantment and dispassion are present, for one who is possessed of the knowledge of disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation possesses its proximate cause.

Bhikkhus, just as when a tree is possessed of branches and foliage, its sprouts reach fulfillment, as do its bark, softwood, and heartwood; in the same way, bhikkhus, when mindfulness and clear comprehension are present, for one who is possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, shame and fear of wrongdoing possess their proximate cause. The First Discourse.

## 3. Mulaka Sutta

"Venerable Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their resort. "Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely; I will speak."

"Yes, Venerable Sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask: 'Friends, in what are all things rooted? In what do all things have their origin? From what do all things arise? Where do all things meet? What is the head of all things?...'"
153:
"If you are asked, 'Bhikkhus, in what are all things rooted? In what do all things originate? From what do all things arise? In what do all things converge? What is the head of all things? What is the governing principle of all things? What is the culmination of all things? What is the essence of all things?'—if you are thus asked by wanderers of other sects, you should answer them in this way:
'Friends, all things are rooted in desire (chanda).
All things originate in attention (manasikāra).
All things arise from contact (phassa).

Bhikkhus, if you are thus asked by wanderers of other sects, you should answer them in this way."
The Third Discourse.
